Chapter 1

Chapter 1 · Verse 1

1.1

नमः श्री-शङ्करानन्द-गुरु-पादाम्बु-जन्मने। सविलास-महा-मोह-ग्राह-ग्रासैक-कर्मणे॥

Salutation to the lotus-like feet of my teacher, Śrī Śaṅkarānanda, whose work is to swallow the crocodile of great delusion and its effects.

Word-for-word
नमः salutation
श्री-शङ्करानन्द-गुरु-पादाम्बु-जन्मने to the lotus feet of Guru Śaṅkarānanda
सविलास-महा-मोह-ग्राह-ग्रासैक-कर्मणे whose sole work is to swallow great delusion with its play

Chapter 1 · Verse 2

1.2

तत्-पादाम्बु-रुह-द्वन्द्व-सेवा-निर्मल-चेतसाम्। सुख-बोधाय तत्त्वस्य विवेदोऽयं विधीयते॥

This discernment of reality is set forth for the clear understanding of those whose minds have been purified through service at their teacher’s two lotus feet.

Word-for-word
तत्-पादाम्बु-रुह-द्वन्द्व-सेवा-निर्मल-चेतसाम् for those whose minds are purified by service to those two lotus feet
सुख-बोधाय for easy understanding
तत्त्वस्य of reality
विवेकः अयम् विधीयते this discernment is set forth

Chapter 1 · Verse 3

1.3

शब्द-स्पर्शादयो वेद्या वैचित्र्याज् जागरे पृथक्। ततो विभक्ता तत्-संविद् ऐक-रूप्यान् न भिद्यते॥

The knowable (vedyas, the sense objects) beginning with sound, touch, etc. are (mistaken as) separate (from each other, i.e., are many) in waking state due to their distinguishing characteristics (vaicitrya), whereas the knower (saṃvid, the I, the consciousness) of these which is distinct from all of them does not differ (i.e., is not many) because of its singular nature (eka-rūpya).

Word-for-word
शब्द-स्पर्श-आदयः sound, touch, and the rest
वेद्याः objects of knowledge
वैचित्र्यात् because of their variety
जागरे पृथक् separate in waking
ततः विभक्ता distinct from them
तत्-संवित् the consciousness that knows them
ऐक-रूप्यात् because it is one in nature
न भिद्यते does not differ

Chapter 1 · Verse 4

1.4

तथा स्वप्नेऽत्र वेद्यं तु न स्थिरं जागरे स्थिरम्। तद्-भेदोऽतस् तयोः संविद् एकरूपा न भिद्यते॥

Similarly in the dream state. Whereas a known object was stable (sthira, remained beyond the moment) in waking, here it is unstable (only as long as its dream thought). Thus there is a difference (in nature) between them (the dream from the waking object). (But) the knower (saṃvid, in both states) having the same nature (eka-rūpā) does not differ (i.e., there is only one I, distinct from those many and different objects).

Word-for-word
तथा स्वप्ने likewise in dream
अत्र वेद्यम् न स्थिरम् here the known is not stable
जागरे स्थिरम् stable in waking
तत्-भेदः अतः therefore the objects differ
तयोः संवित् the consciousness in both
एकरूपा न भिद्यते one in nature, does not differ

Chapter 1 · Verse 5

1.5

सुप्तोत्थितस्य सौषुप्त-तमो-बोधो भवेत् स्मृतिः। सा चावबुद्ध-विषयाऽवबुद्धं तत् तदा तमः॥

For the one waking from deep sleep, there is remembrance (smṛti) that (in dreamless, deep sleep) there was cognition of ignorance (tamas-bodha) in deep sleep (in the form of ‘I knew nothing,’ even time and space disappear there). A (remembrance always) has as its object a (prior) cognition. At that time (in deep sleep), that cognition is (in the form of) tamas (complete ignorance).

Word-for-word
सुप्त-उत्थितस्य of one risen from sleep
सौषुप्त-तमः-बोधः awareness of the darkness of deep sleep
भवेत् स्मृतिः is remembered
सा च and that memory
अवबुद्ध-विषया has what was known as its object
अवबुद्धम् तत् तदा तमः what was known then was ignorance

Chapter 1 · Verse 6

1.6

स बोधो विषयाद् भिन्नो न बोधात् स्वप्न-बोधवत्। एवं स्थान-त्रयेऽप्येका संवित् तत्वद् दिनान्तरे॥

That cognition (bodha, the consciousness, the awareness, the I) is distinct from its object (the complete ignorance in deep sleep), but, like in dream, does not differ from itself. Thus the knower (the consciousness) remains one only in the three states (sthāna-traya, the waking, dream, and deep sleep states) in that same way (as distinct from the changing, but itself unchanging) throughout the day.

Word-for-word
सः बोधः that awareness
विषयात् भिन्नः is distinct from its object
न बोधात् not from awareness itself
स्वप्न-बोधवत् as in dream cognition
एवं स्थान-त्रये अपि thus in all three states
एका संवित् consciousness is one
तत्त्वत् दिनान्तरे likewise through the day

Chapter 1 · Verse 7

1.7

मासाब्द-युग-कल्पेषु गतागम्येष्वनेकधा। नोदेति नास्तम् एत्येका संविद् एषा स्वयं-प्रभा॥

Throughout the countless months, years, ages and world cycles, both past and future, it neither rises (udeti) nor sets (astam eti). This one consciousness (saṃvid) is self shining (svayaṃ-prabhā, and hence, self revealing).

Word-for-word
मास-अब्द-युग-कल्पेषु through months, years, ages, and cosmic cycles
गत-आगम्येषु अनेका through past and future in many ways
न उदेति न अस्तम् एति neither rises nor sets
एका संवित् एषा this one consciousness
स्वयं-प्रभा self-luminous

Chapter 1 · Verse 8

1.8

इयम् आत्मा परानन्दः पर-प्रेमास्पदं यतः। मा न भूवं हि भूयासम् इति प्रेमात्मनीक्ष्यते॥

This (knower, consciousness) is oneself (ātman). It is ultimate fullness (para-ānanda), because it is the natural abode (āspada) of our greatest love (para-preman). Love is seen in the self as, “May I indeed never cease to be,” “May I always be.”

Word-for-word
इयम् आत्मा this is the Self
परानन्दः supreme bliss
पर-प्रेम-आस्पदम् the ground of supreme love
यतः because
मा न भूवम् may I never cease to be
हि भूयासम् may I always be
इति प्रेम आत्मनि ईक्ष्यते thus love is seen directed toward oneself

Chapter 1 · Verse 9

1.9

तत् प्रेमात्मार्थम् अन्यत्र नैवम् अन्यार्थम् आत्मनि। अतस् तत् परमं तेन परमानन्दतात्मनः॥

Only for the sake of oneself is that love (preman) directed towards another, thus love towards oneself is never for the sake of another. Therefore, that (love in oneself) is the highest. Hence the nature of the ultimate fullness (parama-ānandatā) belongs only to the self (ātman, as its abode).

Word-for-word
तत् प्रेम that love
आत्म-अर्थम् is for the sake of the Self
अन्यत्र for another
न एवम् not so
अन्य-अर्थम् for the sake of another
आत्मनि in the Self
अतः therefore
तत् परमम् that is highest
तेन therefore
परमानन्दता आत्मनः the Self is supreme bliss by nature

Chapter 1 · Verse 10

1.10

इत्थं सच्-चित्-परानन्द आत्मा युक्त्या तथाविधम्। परं ब्रह्म तयोश् चैक्यं श्रुत्यन्तेषूपदिश्यते॥

In this way, by this logic, existence-consciousness-fullness (sat-cit-ānanda) is the nature of oneself. Similarly (as existence-consciousness-fullness) is the ultimate brahman (ultimate reality) taught in the śrutis (the Upaniṣads) as the complete identity of these two (oneself and limitless existence-consciousness-fullness).

Word-for-word
इत्थम् thus
सत्-चित्-परानन्द आत्मा the Self is existence, consciousness, and supreme bliss
युक्त्या by reasoning
तथाविधम् परं ब्रह्म the supreme Brahman is of the same nature
तयोः च ऐक्यम् the identity of the two
श्रुत्यन्तेषु उपदिश्यते is taught in the Upaniṣads

Chapter 1 · Verse 11

1.11

अभाने न परं प्रेम भाने न विषये स्पृहा। अतो भानेऽप्यभाताऽसौ परमानन्दतात्मनः॥

If the ultimate fullness nature (parama-ānandatā) of the self was not evident (a-bhāna), there would be no ultimate love. (Yet) if it was (clearly) evident, there would be no attachment (spṛhā) towards the objects of experience (apart from oneself). Therefore, even though (self) evident, it is not (clearly) evident (i.e., it is normally misplaced upon objects of desire).

Word-for-word
अभाने if not manifest
न परं प्रेम there is no supreme love
भाने if manifest
न विषये स्पृहा there is no longing for objects
अतः therefore
भाने अपि अभाता असौ though shining, it appears unshining
परमानन्दता आत्मनः the Self’s nature as supreme bliss

Chapter 1 · Verse 12

1.12

अध्येतृ-वर्ग-मध्यस्थ-पुत्राध्ययन-शब्दवत्। भानेऽप्यभानं भानस्य प्रतिबन्धेन युज्यते॥

Like the chanting voice of one’s child amongst a group of students, even though (the ultimate fullness nature of the self) is evident, in regard to being (distinctly) evident (bhānasya prati), it is (as well) proper to take (yujyate) it as not (clearly) evident (a-bhāna), because of obstruction (pratibandha, because of its misplacement on objects of experience).

Word-for-word
अध्येतृ-वर्ग-मध्यस्थ among a group of students
पुत्र-अध्ययन-शब्दवत् like the sound of one’s child reciting
भाने अपि अभानम् non-recognition despite being present
भानस्य प्रतिबन्धेन through an obstruction to recognition
युज्यते is explained

Chapter 1 · Verse 13

1.13

प्रतिबन्धोऽस्ति-भातीति-व्यवहारार्ह-वस्तुनि। तन्-निरस्य विरुद्धस्य तस्योत्पादनम् उच्यते॥

Toward any object is applicable the experience, “It (the existence) is” and it (the awareness) is evident” (asti-bhāti), (yet) there is an obstruction said to be the rejecting of this (tan-nirasya) and imposing its opposite (experience, “I am not their existence” and “I am not their appearance”).

Word-for-word
प्रतिबन्धः obstruction
अस्ति-भाति इति ‘exists and shines’
व्यवहार-अर्ह-वस्तुनि for an object fit for ordinary experience
तत् निरस्य rejecting that
विरुद्धस्य तस्य its opposite
उत्पादनम् the superimposition
उच्यते is called

Chapter 1 · Verse 14

1.14

तस्य हेतुः समानाभिहारः पुत्र-ध्वनि-श्रुतौ। इहानादिर् अविद्यैव व्यामोहैक-निबन्धनम्॥

The reason for that (obstruction) in regard to hearing the voice of one’s child is the mingling together as the same (samāna-abhihāra, with the other voices). Here, (the reason) is beginningless (uncaused) ignorance (a-vidyā, ignorance of one’s nature as the only limitless existence, consciousness). That alone is the obstruction leading to confusion (that things exist and appear independent of my existence-consciousness, i.e., that they independently exist and are not me).

Word-for-word
तस्य हेतुः its cause
समान-अभिहारः confusion through mingling with similar sounds
पुत्र-ध्वनि-श्रुतौ when hearing one’s child’s voice
इह here
अनादिः अविद्या एव beginningless ignorance alone
व्यामोह-एक-निबन्धनम् is the sole basis of delusion

Chapter 1 · Verse 15

1.15

चिद्-आनन्दमय-ब्रह्म-प्रतिबिम्ब-समन्विता। तमो-रजस्-सत्व-गुणा प्रकृतिर् द्विविधा च सा॥

Prakṛti (mother nature) consists of the three guṇas (attributes): tamas (density, ignorance, etc.), rajas (activity, agitation, etc.), and sattva (clarity, knowledge, etc.). It is imbued with a reflection (pratibimba, semblance, appearance) of brahman consisting of consciousness-fullness. This prakṛti has two forms (as follows).

Word-for-word
चित्-आनन्द-मय-ब्रह्म-प्रतिबिम्ब-समन्विता joined with a reflection of Brahman, whose nature is consciousness and bliss
तमस्-रजस्-सत्त्व-गुणा having the qualities of tamas, rajas, and sattva
प्रकृतिः द्विविधा च सा that prakṛti is twofold

Chapter 1 · Verse 16

1.16

सत्व-शुद्ध्यविशुद्धिभ्यां मायाऽविद्ये च ते मते। माया-बिम्बो वशी-कृत्य तां स्यात् सर्वज्ञ ईश्वरः॥

From the perspective of its pure sattva alone, it (prakṛti) is called ‘māyā’ (appearance, in every mind, presenting a varied world). From the perspective of its impurity (a-viśuddhi, with rajas and tamas also), it is called ‘a-vidyā’ (individual ignorance, taking all these appearances as real). ‘Īśvara’ (the Lord) is the (brahman) presence (bimba) in that (sattva only aspect) māyā, controlling (vaśī-kṛtya, as pure intelligence, cosmic order) that (prakṛti), and (thus) is all-knowing (sarva-jña).

Word-for-word
सत्त्व-शुद्धि-अविशुद्धिभ्याम् by purity and impurity of sattva
माया-अविद्ये called māyā and avidyā
च ते मते these are the two
माया-बिम्बः the reflection in māyā
वशी-कृत्य ताम् having brought it under control
स्यात् सर्वज्ञः ईश्वरः becomes the all-knowing Lord

Chapter 1 · Verse 17

1.17

अविद्या-वशगस् त्वन्यस् तद्-वैचित्र्याद् अनेकधा। सा कारण-शरीरं स्यात् प्राज्ञस् तत्राभिमानवान्॥

But the other (the jīva, the individual, the brahman presence in a-vidyā) is under the spell of a-vidyā, and, because of the variety (of rajas and tamas mixtures) in that (a-vidyā) is taken as many (as a plurality of jīvas). This (a-vidyā) is the causal body (kāraṇa-śarīra), and is the one who is identified in that (causal body). That is, (having not been able to distinguish itself from its ignorant notions about itself) it is called the ‘prājña’ (the knower consciousness, and in a daily context it is the deep sleeper).* *(But contextually here, it is this knower consciousness immersed in a-vyakta, the unmanifest, ready to awaken by its karma to a continuance of its jiva-hood, its individuality, once the world of experience re-manifests.)

Word-for-word
अविद्या-वशगः तु अन्यः the other is subject to ignorance
तद्-वैचित्र्यात् because of its variety
अनेकधा in many forms
सा कारण-शरीरम् that is the causal body
प्राज्ञः तत्र अभिमानवान् the one identified with it is prājña

Chapter 1 · Verse 18

1.18

तमः-प्रधान-प्रकृतेस् तद्-भोगायेश्वराज्ञया। वियत्-पवन-तेजो-ऽम्बु-भुवो भूतानि जज्ञिरे॥

Per the (karma) order wielded by the Lord, for the (earned) experiences of that (jīva), from (the then unbalanced three guṇas wherein) tamas predominance of the aspects of prakṛti were born (in their subtle form) the elements (bhūtas): space (viyat, ‘reaching everywhere’, dimension), wind (pavana, movement), fire (tejas, heat and light), water (ambu, fluidity, chemical bonding remaining while in movement), and earth (bhū, solidity, granularity, gravity).

Word-for-word
तमः-प्रधान-प्रकृतेः from prakṛti in which tamas predominates
तत्-भोगाय for its experience
ईश्वर-आज्ञया by the Lord’s command
वियत्-पवन-तेजः-अम्बु-भुवः space, air, fire, water, and earth
भूतानि जज्ञिरे the elements were born

Chapter 1 · Verse 19

1.19

सत्वांशैः पञ्चभिस् तेषां क्रमाद् धीन्द्रिय-पञ्चकम्। श्रोत्र-त्वग्-अक्षि-रसन-घ्राणाख्यम् उपजायते॥

From the sattva (knowledge) aspect of each of these five (elements) are indeed born separately (kramāt – not as a whole) the five sensory organs (indriyas) called: hearing (from the sattva, knowing, aspect of the subtle element space, dimension), touching (from the sattva aspect of the subtle element wind, movement), (similarly) seeing, tasting, and smelling.

Word-for-word
सत्त्व-अंशैः पञ्चभिः तेषाम् from the five sattva portions of those elements
क्रमात् in order
धी-इन्द्रिय-पञ्चकम् the five organs of knowledge
श्रोत्र-त्वक्-अक्षि-रसना-घ्राण-आख्यम् called hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell
उपजायते arise

Chapter 1 · Verse 20

1.20

तैर् अन्तः-करणं सर्वैर् वृत्ति-भेदेन तद् द्विधा। मनो विमर्श-रूपं स्याद् बुद्धिः स्यान् निश्चयात्मिका॥

From (the sattva aspect of) all these (elements – as a whole, not separately) is (born) the antaḥ-karaṇa (the internal organ, the mind in all its facets) with different forms and functions (vṛtti-bheda, different thoughts that make up the mind). That (internal organ) is of two types. One type is called the manas (the mind in charge of the senses) where the thoughts have the nature of vimarśa (examination, consideration, reflection, i.e., fact finding the pros and cons of what the senses present while trying to make some sense out of the data). The other type is buddhi (the intellect, the mind in charge of knowledge) where the thoughts have the nature of niścaya (ascertainment, decision, conviction).

Word-for-word
तैः सर्वैः from all of them
अन्तः-करणम् the inner organ
वृत्ति-भेदेन by difference of function
तत् द्विधा it is twofold
मनः विमर्श-रूपम् manas has the nature of deliberation
स्यात् बुद्धिः and buddhi is
निश्चय-आत्मिका of the nature of ascertainment

Chapter 1 · Verse 21

1.21

रजोंशैः पञ्चभिस् तेषां क्रमात् कर्मेन्द्रयाणि तु। वाक्-पाणि-पाद-पायुपस्थाभिधानानि जज्ञिरे॥

From the rajas (activity) aspect of the five (elements) separately (kramāt – not as a whole, (Sarva Vedānta Siddhānta Sara Saṅgraha) & (Tattva Bodha)) are born the five organs of action (karmendriyas, the powers of action) called: voicing (vāc, via vocal cords, etc., from space), handling (pāṇi, via hands, etc., from wind), moving (pāda, via feet, legs, from fire), excreting (pāyu, via the anus, etc., from water), and procreating (upa-stha, via the penis, etc., from earth).

Word-for-word
रजः-अंशैः पञ्चभिः तेषाम् from the five rajas portions of those elements
क्रमात् in order

Chapter 1 · Verse 22

From (the rajas aspect of) all these (elements) as a whole (sahita – not separately) comes the prāṇa (life energy, animating energy), which is of five types due to different forms and functions (vṛtti-bheda) called: outward energy (prāṇa, via outward breathing, etc.), downward energy (apāna, via inward breathing, etc.), assimilating energy (samāna, via digestion, etc.), upward energy (upāna, via retching, ejecting the prāṇa from the body, etc.), and circulating energy (vyāna, via circulatory system, etc.).

Chapter 1 · Verse 25

The Lord (as Hiraṇya-garbha, the initial cosmic person) is the totality (samaṣṭi) of all this (which has becomes this universe) due to the sense of identification (tādātmya-vedana) in all of their natures, sva-ātman, their subtle bodies, (or, rather in His cosmic subtle body). The one who is other than that one, though, in the absence of that (identification in the total) they (the wise) call the individual knower (vyaṣṭi-saṃjña, who knows little, simply by this one’s identification only with this individual body, instead of with the totality).

Chapter 1 · Verse 26

1.26

तद्-भोगाय पुनर्-भोग्य-भोगायतन-जन्मने। पञ्ची-करोति भगवान् प्रयेकं वियद्-आदिकम्॥

To provide objects of experiences for those (individual subtle bodies), and provide for births into more fit receptacles of these experiences (punar-bhogya-bhoga-āyatana-janmas), the Lord (bhagavat) mixed each one (of these elements), beginning with space, five-fold*. As an example, the subtle principal of space is dimension, whereas our common parlance of experience and understanding of space is mostly the outer space beyond the atmosphere, which has relative minor percentages of movement, heat and light, liquidity, and solidity. Currently outer space is understood, per Wikipedia, as a hard vacuum containing a low density of particles, predominantly a plasma of hydrogen and helium, as well as electromagnetic radiation, magnetic fields, neutrinos, dust, and cosmic rays, and having a baseline temperature of about 2.7 °C above absolute zero temperature. Similarly, the subtle principle of wind is movement, whereas our experience and understanding of wind is the atmosphere as being predominantly movement or circulation, and relatively less amount of dimension compared to outer space, as well as of the other three elements present in the atmosphere. This is certainly a reasonably intelligent understanding of our entire universe, not displaced, though for other purposes elaborated upon by our current sciences. It’s good enough here to then understand how this universe can be completely subordinated because of its dependencies to the more unifying principles first of my mind, then the Lord’s mind [Hiraṇya-garbha], and finally the one existence-consciousness.)

Word-for-word

पुनः-भोग्य-भोग-आयतन-जन्मने to produce objects, enjoyment, and places of experience
पञ्ची-करोति performs quintuplication
भगवान् the Lord
प्रत्येकम् वियत्-आदिकम् each element beginning with space

Chapter 1 · Verse 27

1.27

द्विधा विधाय चैकैकं चतुर्धा प्रथमं पुनः। स्वस्वेतर-द्वितीयांशैर् योजनात् पञ्च पञ्च ते॥

(The five-folding to make one gross element is) proportioning into two portions and then the first portion into four portions*, so that the second (predominant) portion is (the one subtle element) itself alone and each of the other four portions are the other (subtle elements). From this combination (yogana) there are five (gross elements) each consisting of five (subtle elements, with each gross element being called its predominant subtle element component). The confusion is that dividing an element would leave a portion of itself in the first half, but, not mentioned, that half loses its element and then is replaced by quarter, at this point eighth, portions with each of the other elements. The end result would be only five gross elements of exactly half itself and one-eighth each the other four, leaving no variety within each gross element. The better understanding is to take ‘into two’ as describing a predominance of itself for each element, with the balance ‘into four’ as minority portions for the other elements. So we don’t necessarily have five unique gross elements, but a spectrum of higher and lesser predominance of dimension, movement, etc. in different locations which, through our senses, the mind then names as more or less spacious, more or less gaseous, etc.)

Word-for-word
द्विधा विधाय dividing in two
च एकैकम् each one
चतुर्धा प्रथमम् पुनः then dividing the first part into four
स्व-स्व-इतर-द्वितीय-अंशैः with the secondary portions of the other elements
योजनात् by combination
पञ्च पञ्च ते thus each of the five is fivefold

Hiraṇya-garbha (the knower reflected in the total subtle body) is then present in this (cosmic) gross (element body, who can then be called Virāj as the knower therein).* In the (individual’s) body it would be called the vaiśvā-nara (the common-world knower, the individual who can now experience the common manifest world, who awakens to the manifest day of experiences). The answer manufactured here is directed to mature adults, but is not completely unlike the answer to children that it was a stork who brought you to us – it is what the recipient can find helpful for the time being).

Chapter 1 · Verse 41

1.41

सुषुप्त्यभाने भानं तु समाधावात्मानोऽन्वयः। व्यतिरेकस् त्वात्म-भाने सुषुप्त्यनवभासनम्॥

Whereas, in samādhi* (contemplation where there is only awareness that is oneself and no separation of knower-known) which is also without suṣupti (deep sleep), there is the anvaya, (continued presence, of the self, of existence-awareness alone). And the non-appearance of deep sleep (as well as of the causal ignorance of the prājña, ) while the self is manifestly present is (said to be) its vyatireka (co-absence, of the unmanifest, as well as one’s causal body without modification of moda, degrees of pleasure , while the self independently continues). When the mind in nididhyāsana eventually either drops cognizance of a separation between meditator-meditating-meditated, or comes to, at least for a time, doubtlessly appreciate the unreality of a distinction of meditator-meditating-meditated, even though they still appear in the mind, this may be called samādhi within nididhyāsana. And the Bhagavad Gītā sanctions this use of the term samādhi, (Bhagavad Gītā). Even the yoga tradition acknowledges that one arrives at samādhi through dhāraṇā and dhyāna, (Yoga Sūtras). We can take nididhyāsana, including the more general term dhyāna, as encompassing dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi, when the contemplated relates to oneself as brahman.)

Word-for-word
सुषुप्ति-अभाने when deep sleep is absent
भानम् तु the presence
समाधौ आत्मनः of the Self in samādhi
अन्वयः is co-presence
व्यतिरेकः तु and co-absence
आत्म-भाने when the Self shines
सुषुप्ति-अनवभासनम् deep sleep does not appear

Chapter 1 · Verse 42

1.42

यथा मुञ्जाद् इषीकैवम् आत्मा युक्त्या समुद्धृतः। शरीर-त्रितयाद् धीरैः परं ब्रह्मैव जायते॥

Like the internal pith (iṣīkā, for making the upanāyana ceremonial waistband is separated with care) from the muñja grass, so the ātman is carefully separated by the wise (dhīras) with (the help of this teaching and supporting) logic (yukti) from (the kośas of) the three bodies (the gross, subtle, and causal bodies). Then one is (as though) reborn as the ultimate brahman alone (no longer limited by these kośas).

Word-for-word
यथा मुञ्जात् इषीका एवम् as the pith is drawn from muñja grass
आत्मा the Self
युक्त्या समुद्धृतः is extracted by reasoning
शरीर-त्रितयात् from the three bodies
धीरैः by the wise
परम् ब्रह्म एव जायते one becomes supreme Brahman alone

Chapter 1 · Verse 43

1.43

परापरात्मनोर् एवं युक्त्या संभावितैकता। तत् त्वम् अस्यादि-वाक्यैस् सा भाग-त्यागेन लक्ष्यते॥

In this way is manifestly taught (saṃbhāvitā) with (the help of) logic one’s identity with the para-ātman (unlimited self) from the a-para-ātman (imagined limited self, as these kośas). (Similarly) this (identity) is indicated (lakṣyate) by eliminating (unequal) aspects (bhāga-tyāga) through the (mahā-)vākyas (pithy declarations from the Upaniṣads), such as ‘tat tvam asi’ (‘that you are’), etc. (see )

पर-अपर-आत्मनोः of the higher and lower Self
एवम् युक्त्या thus through reasoning
संभावित-एकता their unity is established
तत् त्वम् असि-आदि-वाक्यैः by statements such as ‘That thou art’
सा that unity
भाग-त्यागेन by giving up the incompatible parts
लक्ष्यते is indicated

Chapter 1 · Verse 44

1.44

जगतो यद् उपादानं मायाम् आदाय तामसीम्। निमित्तं शुद्ध-सत्त्वां ताम् उच्यते ब्रह्म तद्-गिरा॥

By the word ‘tad’ (‘that’) is referenced brahman which has taken on māyā through her (predominantly) tamas (darkness) aspect which would be the material cause (upādāna) of the universe and through her pure sattva (knowledge) aspect which would be the intelligent cause (nimitta, of the universe).

Word-for-word

यत् उपादानम् that which is the material cause
मायाम् आदाय तामसीम् assuming māyā’s tamasic aspect
निमित्तम् the efficient cause
शुद्ध-सत्त्वाम् pure sattva
ताम् उच्यते ब्रह्म तद्-गिरा that is called Brahman by the word ‘That’

Chapter 1 · Verse 45

1.45

यदा मलिन-सत्त्वां तां काम-कर्मादि-दूषिताम्। आदत्ते तत् परं ब्रह्म त्वं-पदेन तदोच्यते॥

By the word ‘tvam’ (‘you’) is referenced that same ultimate brahman, whenever it has taken on (māyā’s) sattva (knowledge aspect) mixed up (malina, with rajas and tamas, and thus limited) and (thus) defiled with desires and activities (to fulfill them), etc.

आदत्ते assumes
तत् परम् ब्रह्म then the supreme Brahman
त्वं-पदेन by the word ‘you’
तदा उच्यते is indicated

Chapter 1 · Verse 46

1.46

त्रितयीम् अपि तां मुक्त्वा परस्-पर-विरोधिनीम्। अखण्डं सच्-चिद्-आनन्दं महा-वाक्येन लक्ष्यते॥

But eliminating these three features (tāmasī māyā upādānam plus the śuddha-sattvā māyā nimittam, and malina-sattvā māyā dūṣitā) that are incompatible with each other, no distinction (between tat and tvam, the Lord and myself) is indicated by this mahā-vākya (‘tat tvam asi’), which is their (compatible nature as) existence-consciousness-fullness (sat-cit-ānanda)*. Permanency can only be brought about by knowledge, because it is factual. Nevertheless, one has to be emotionally stable for this knowledge to assimilate to the core of one’s being and not rejected because of one’s low self opinions about the body, emotions, and intellect.)

Word-for-word

मुक्त्वा setting aside
परस्पर-विरोधिनीम् which are mutually opposed
अखण्डम् सत्-चित्-आनन्दम् undivided existence-consciousness-bliss
महा-वाक्येन by the great statement
लक्ष्यते is indicated

Chapter 1 · Verse 47

1.47

सोऽयम्-इत्यादि-वाक्येषु विरोधात् तद्-इदन्तयोः। त्यागेन भागयोर् एक आश्रयो लक्ष्यते यथा॥

The same as in declarations such as, ‘That (past location Devadatta person) is this (present Devadatta person)’, by eliminating the two (incompatible) features (bhāgayoḥ tyāgena), in the form of ‘that’ and ‘this’, then the one basis (āśraya, ‘is Devadatta’) is indicated.

विरोधात् because of the contradiction
तत्-इदन्तयोः between ‘that’ and ‘this’
त्यागेन भागयोः by relinquishing the conflicting parts
एकः आश्रयः one underlying basis
लक्ष्यते is indicated
यथा as (in the example)

Chapter 1 · Verse 48

1.48

मायाऽविद्ये विहायैवम् उपाधी पर-जीवयोः। अखण्डं सच्-चिद्-आनन्दं पर ब्रह्मैव लक्ष्यते॥

Eliminating (negating) both māyā and a-vidya (the cosmic and the not-knowing-individual) upādhis (apparently limiting adjuncts) of the Lord and the jīva (respectively), their non-distinction (a-khaṇḍa) is indicated as brahman only, which is their (compatible nature as) existence-consciousness-fullness.

Chapter 1 · Verse 49

1.49

स-विकल्पस्य लक्ष्यत्वे लक्ष्यस्य स्याद् अवस्तुता। निर्-विकल्पस्य लक्ष्यत्वं न दृष्टं न च सम्भवि॥

(Objection:) If the nature of what is being indicated (lakṣyatva) is sa-vikalpa (having apparent features, the upādhis, not its real, essential nature), then the indicated lacks (independent) reality (apart from those features). But if the nature of what is being indicated is nir-vikalpa (having no apparent features), then (the indicated) is neither seen (dṛṣṭa, to the senses) nor (logically) possible (sambhavin, to the mind).

Word-for-word
स-विकल्पस्य of what has distinctions
लक्ष्यत्वे if it is the object indicated
लक्ष्यस्य of the indicated object
स्यात् अवस्तुता there would be unreality
निर्-विकल्पस्य of what is distinctionless
लक्ष्यत्वम् being the object indicated
न दृष्टम् not seen
न च सम्भवि nor possible

Chapter 1 · Verse 50

1.50

विकल्पो निर्-विकल्पस्य स-विकल्पस्य वा भवेत्। आद्ये व्याहतिर् अन्यत्रानवस्थाऽत्माश्रयादयः॥

(Reply, assuming the above two objections are true:) If (brahman) having no features (nir-vikalpa) can (by the senses or mind) be figured out (vikalpa, can be featured), then this starts out as (an unresolvable) contradiction (vyāhati). If (brahman) having features can be figured out, then there will be (various logical fallacies, such as) anyatra-an-avasthā (mutual dependence, i.e., if the known features are dependent upon an unknown brahman, then the features are not fully known, and may themselves be equally unreal, if brahman happens to be unreal) or ātma-āśraya (self dependence, i.e., if brahman is completely independent from the features, then the features will tell us nothing about an unknown brahman), etc.

Word-for-word
विकल्पः conceptual distinction
निर्-विकल्पस्य वा स-विकल्पस्य of what is distinctionless or qualified
भवेत् would arise
आद्ये in the first case
व्याहतिः there is contradiction
अन्यत्र in the other case
अनवस्था-आत्म-आश्रय-आदयः infinite regress, self-dependence, and the like

Chapter 1 · Verse 51

1.51

इदं गुण-क्रिया-जाति-द्रव्य-सम्बन्ध-वस्तुषु। समं तेन स्व-रूपस्य सर्वम् एतद् इतीष्यताम्॥

This same (idaṃ samam, uncertainty would then apply) towards any object (vastu) having a quality, having an action, having a category, having a substance, and having a relationship (i.e., the relative things of the world would only be relatively known). Hence, it is instead to be understood (through the authority of the scriptural teaching) that all this (relative and thus not absolutely real universe) is (superimposed) upon my very (undismissible, definitely real) nature (sva-rūpa, by experience as existence-consciousness, and by scripture, as limitless).

Word-for-word
इदम् this
गुण-क्रिया-जाति-द्रव्य-सम्बन्ध-वस्तुषु for things with qualities, actions, kinds, substances, and relations
समम् equally
तेन therefore
स्व-रूपस्य of one’s own nature
सर्वम् एतत् all this
इति ईष्यताम् let it be understood

Chapter 1 · Verse 52

1.52

विकल्प-तद्-अभावाभ्याम् असंस्पृष्टात्म-वस्तुनि। विकल्पितत्व-लक्ष्यत्व-सम्बन्धाद्यास् तु कल्पिताः॥

When the reality of the self is untouched by either (the presence of superimposed) attributes or the lack of them, then the nature of being attributed, of being logically indicated, of having any relationships, etc. are all assumptions (kalpatā vṛttis, imposed by our mind on one’s self, the knower of the mind).

Chapter 1 · Verse 53

1.53

इत्थं वाक्यैस् तद्-अर्थानुसन्धानं श्रवणं भवेत्। युक्त्या सम्भावितत्वानुसन्धानं मननं तु तत्॥

Thus, what is called śravaṇa (listening to the teaching) involves scrutiny as to its meaning intended by these statements (mahā-vākyas). Whereas, manana (understanding) should involve scrutiny as to its validity (towards oneself and one’s life) by means of logic (yukti).

Chapter 1 · Verse 55

1.55

ध्यातृ-ध्याने परित्यज्य क्रमाद् ध्येयैक-गोचरम्। निवात-दीपवच् चित्तं समाधिर् अभिधीयते॥

In stages (kramāt, where initially one starts with a distinction of knower-knowing-known), eliminating (the notion of a distinction) as an agent and the action of meditating, where the mind, like a flame protected from the (vacillations of the) wind, has as its scope only the one dhyeya (the contemplated, self as limitless existence-consciousness, unswayed by doubts), is called samādhi (staying put only in oneself).

1.57

Chapter 1 · Verse 59

1.59

Chapter 1 · Verse 61

Chapter 1 · Verse 63

1.63

परोक्षं ब्रह्म-विज्ञानं शाब्दं देशिक-पूर्वकम्। बुद्धि-पूर्व-कृतं पापं कृत्स्नं दहति वह्निवत्॥

The assimilated knowledge (vijñāna) of brahman (limitless existence-consciousness, i.e., as oneself), which was (previously) indirect (parokṣa, as belonging to the Lord) and which was introduced by a teacher (deśika-pūrva, who can only point to the truth, not ‘give’ you the truth) through words (sābda, i.e., indirectly) – now, like a fire, completely burns up the pāpa (all karma, good or bad, that kept you in cycles of rebirths) committed prior to this knowledge.

Word-for-word
परोक्षम् indirect
ब्रह्म-विज्ञानम् knowledge of Brahman
शाब्दम् arising from words
देशिक-पूर्वकम् initiated by a teacher
बुद्धि-पूर्व-कृतम् deliberately committed
पापम् कृत्स्नम् all wrongdoing
दहति burns
वह्निवत् like fire

Chapter 1 · Verse 64

1.64

अपरोक्षात्म-विज्ञानं शाब्दं देशिक-पूर्वकम्। संसार-कारणाज्ञान-तमसश् चण्ड-भास्करः॥

The assimilated knowledge (vijñāna), having the nature of not being out of reach of one’s experience (a-parokṣa), which was introduced by a teacher (as someone required to guide and clarify your way in the scripture) through their words (sābda), like the bright light of the sun, (leads you) out of the darkness of ignorance that is the material cause of saṃsāra (unbecoming becoming).

Word-for-word
अपरोक्ष-आत्म-विज्ञानम् direct knowledge of the Self
शाब्दम् arising from the teaching
देशिक-पूर्वकम् given by a teacher’s instruction
संसार-कारण-अज्ञान-तमसः the darkness of ignorance, cause of saṃsāra
चण्ड-भास्करः is the fierce sun

Chapter 1 · Verse 65

1.65

इत्थं तत्त्व-विवेकं विधाय विधिवन्-मनस् समाधाय। विगलित-संसृति-बन्धः प्राप्नोति परं पदं नरो न चिरात्॥

Thus, one starts distinguishing through tattva-viveka (discernment of reality, from ignorance, from māyā and her effects, such as the pañca-koṣas) and begins to settle the instructed mind (in that reality). Before long, the retained notions of bondage come to an end and the person attains the ultimate abode (paraṃ padam, brahman only as oneself).

Word-for-word
इत्थम् thus
तत्त्व-विवेकम् discernment of reality
विधाय having made
विधिवत् properly
मनः समाधाय settling the mind
विगलित-संसृति-बन्धः freed from the bond of transmigration
प्राप्नोति attains
परम् पदम् the highest state
नरः न चिरात् a person, before long

Chapter 2

Chapter 2 · Verse 1

2.1

सद्-अद्वैतं श्रुतं यत् तत् पञ्च-भूत-विवेकतः। बोद्धुं शक्यं ततो भूत-पञ्चकं प्रविविच्यते॥

That non-dual Being, stated in śruti, can be known by discrimination of the five elements. Therefore the five elements are examined in detail.

Word-for-word
सद्-अद्वैतम् non-dual Being
श्रुतम् stated in śruti
यत् which
तत् that
पञ्च-भूत-विवेकतः by discrimination of the five elements
बोद्धुम् to know
शक्यम् is possible
ततः therefore
भूत-पञ्चकम् the five elements
प्रविविच्यते is examined in detail
Expanded source translation

Since that (brahman), which is said to be non-dual reality according to scripture (śruta), can be known by distinguishing (it) from the five elements (pañca-bhūta-viveka), then the nature of the five elements is now pointed out in more detail.

Chapter 2 · Verse 2

2.2

शब्द-स्पर्शौ रूप-रसौ गन्धो भूत-गुणा इमे। एक-द्वि-त्रि-चतुः-पञ्च-गुणा व्योमादिषु क्रमात्॥

Sound and touch, form and taste, smell: these are the qualities of the elements. In those beginning with space, the qualities are one, two, three, four, and five, in order.

Word-for-word
शब्द-स्पर्शौ sound and touch
रूप-रसौ form and taste
गन्धः smell
भूत-गुणाः qualities of the elements
इमे these
एक-द्वि-त्रि-चतुः-पञ्च-गुणाः having one, two, three, four, and five qualities
व्योम-आदिषु in space and the rest
क्रमात् in order
Expanded source translation

The properties (guṇas, perceived by the senses) of the (gross) elements are sound (from space, as dimension, sensed by the organ of hearing through the ears), touch (from wind, movement, sensed by the organ of touch throughout the surfaces of the body), form (from fire, as heat and light, sensed by sight through the eyes), taste (from water, as liquidity, sensed by the organ of taste primarily through the tongue), and smell (from earth, as solidity, sensed by the organ of smell through the nose). These guṇas in space, etc. are accumulatively (kramāt, by five-fold physicalizing, ) one (guṇa, in space), two (guṇas, i.e., sound and touch, in wind), (similarly) three, four and five (respectively in the other three elements).

Chapter 2 · Verse 3

2.3

प्रति-ध्वनिर् वियच्-छब्दो वायौ बीसीति शब्दनम्। अनुष्णा-शीत-संस्पर्शः वह्नौ भुगु-भुगु-ध्वनिः॥

Echo is the sound of space. In wind is the sound “bīsī”; its touch is neither hot nor cold. In fire is the sound “bhugu-bhugu.”

Word-for-word
प्रति-ध्वनिः echo
वियत्-शब्दः sound of space
वायौ in wind
बीसी-इति “bīsī,” thus
शब्दनम् sound
अनुष्ण-शीत-संस्पर्शः touch that is neither hot nor cold
वह्नौ in fire
भुगु-भुगु-ध्वनिः “bhugu-bhugu” sound
Expanded source translation

An echo is a sound in space (viyat, dimension, properly it is that which is the medium that allows sound waves to exist and travel). In wind is sound, such as ‘bīsi’ (a whooshing soundalike, made by the movement of air in space), and touch which is (intrinsically) neither cold nor hot, i.e., has not the qualities of fire, etc.). In fire is sound, such as ‘bhugu-bhugu’ (a cracking soundalike)…

Chapter 2 · Verse 4

2.4

उष्णः स्पर्शः प्रभा-रूपं जले बुलु-बुलु-ध्वनिः। शीतः स्पर्शः शुक्ल-रूपं रसो माधूर्यम् ईरितः॥

Hot is touch; radiance is form. In water is the sound “bulu-bulu.” Cold is touch; white is form; sweetness is said to be taste.

स्पर्शः touch
प्रभा-रूपम् radiance as form
जले in water
बुलु-बुलु-ध्वनिः “bulu-bulu” sound
शीतः cold
स्पर्शः touch
शुक्ल-रूपम् white form
रसः taste
माधूर्यम् sweetness
ईरितः is said
Expanded source translation

…Also (fire, i.e., heat and light) has (the sensed qualities) touch (from wind) and heat (from itself). In water (liquidity) is sound, such as ‘bulu-bulu’ (a gurgling soundalike), and (has a sensed) touch (from wind), a cool temperature and clear color (from fire), and produces (īrita) a refreshing taste (from itself as clean water)…

Chapter 2 · Verse 5

2.5

भूमौ कडकडाशब्दः काठिन्यं स्पर्श इष्यते। नीलादिकं चित्र-रूपं मधुराम्लादिको रसः॥

On earth is the sound “kaḍakaḍa.” Hardness is said to be touch. Blue and the like are varied forms; sweet, sour, and the like are tastes.

कडकडा-शब्दः “kaḍakaḍa” sound
काठिन्यम् hardness
स्पर्शः touch
इष्यते is considered
नील-आदिकम् blue and the like
चित्र-रूपम् varied form
मधुर-अम्ल-आदिकः sweet, sour, and the like
रसः taste
Expanded source translation

…In earth (solidity) is sound, such as ‘kaḍa-kaḍā’ (a rumbling soundalike). It produces a solid touch (from contact), a varied color, such as blue, etc. (from fire via sight), a sweet, sour, etc. taste (from liquidity via the taste buds)…

Chapter 2 · Verse 6

2.6

सुरभी-तर-गन्धौ द्वौ गुणाः सम्यग् विवेचिताः। श्रोत्रं त्वक् चक्षुषि जिह्वा घ्राणं चेन्द्रिय-पञ्चकम्॥

Two smells—fragrant and other—are distinguished. Hearing, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose are the five senses.

Word-for-word
सुरभी-इतर-गन्धौ fragrant and other smells
द्वौ two
गुणाः qualities
सम्यक् properly
विवेचिताः distinguished
श्रोत्रम् hearing
त्वक् skin
चक्षुषि eyes
जिह्वा tongue
घ्राणम् smell, nose
च and
इन्द्रिय-पञ्चकम् the five senses
Expanded source translation

…Also (in earth) are pleasant and unpleasant smells (from itself). (In this way) are the qualities (of the five elements via the senses) discerned (from each other). The five sense organs are hearing (via ears), touch (via the nerved skin surfaces on and inside the body), sight (via the eyes), taste (via the taste buds on the tongue), and smell (via the nose).

Chapter 2 · Verse 7

2.7

कर्णादि-गोलकस्थं तच् छब्दादि-ग्राहकं क्रमात्। सौक्ष्म्यात् कार्यानुमेयं तत् प्रायो धावेद्-बहिर्-मुखम्॥

That [sense], dwelling in the ear and the other receptacles, grasps sound and the rest in order. Because it is subtle, it is inferred from its effects; it usually moves outward.

Word-for-word
कर्ण-आदि the ear and the rest
गोलक-स्थम् dwelling in the receptacle
तत् that
शब्द-आदि sound and the rest
ग्राहकम् grasping
क्रमात् in order
सौक्ष्म्यात् because of subtlety
कार्य-अनुमेयम् inferred from effects
तत् it
प्रायः usually
धावेत् moves
बहिर्-मुखम् outward
Expanded source translation

Each one of these has a receptor apparatus (golakas), starting with the ears (skin, etc.), that are connected to the (sense organ) graspers (of the elements’ guṇas) starting with sound, etc. in the same order (as their predominant subtle to grosser element). Due to (the sense organs’) subtility (saukṣmya, being made only of sattva guṇa and being dependent upon their gross receptor apparatus, and thus not perceptible to these senses), each one is only inferred (by our mind, based upon their effects on the mind). Generally they (the senses) move outwards (into the world of the objects)*. *(For example, the sense of hearing perceives outwards towards the direction of the source of a sound, and sight perceives outwards to reach a perceivable form and perceives its direction and distance. Even though our modern sciences infer that the sound and light waves enter inward to the receptor apparatuses, indeed our experience is that the mind starts from you out through respective sense organ to its object.)

Chapter 2 · Verse 12

2.12

मनो दशेन्द्रियाध्यक्षं हृत्-पद्म-गोलके स्थितम्। तच् चान्तःकरणं बाह्येष्वस्वातन्त्र्याद् विनेन्द्रियैः॥

The mind, ruler of the ten senses, is situated in the receptacle of the heart-lotus. It is the inner instrument because, without the senses, it lacks independence regarding external things.

Word-for-word
मनः mind
दश-इन्द्रिय-अध्यक्षम् ruler of the ten senses
हृत्-पद्म-गोलके in the heart-lotus receptacle
स्थितम् situated
तत् that
च and
अन्तः-करणम् inner instrument
बाह्येषु regarding external things
अस्वातन्त्र्यात् because of lacking independence
विना without
इन्द्रियैः the senses
Expanded source translation

The internal organ (antaḥ-karaṇa) is (in general called) the manas (the ‘mind’, which includes all thoughts that can be divided between examining thoughts or knowing thoughts, and those can be further divided into emotions, egos, memories, etc.). It is the overseer (adhy-akṣa) of the ten organs (of sensing and action, as part of its examining job). It is located in the lotus-like heart (hṛd, the center of the person, which is felt to be ‘working’ day and night) as its golaka (its apparatus)*. Because it lacks independence (a-svātantrya) from the (five) senses in regard to external (objects), then it is called ‘internal’. *(We may now say that the brain is the apparatus, but no arguing that if the choice is whether someone remains alive or not, it is the heart, not the brain that determines whether the subtle body remains in the body. And, one can be brain-dead, but still alive as long as the heart keeps beating.)

Chapter 2 · Verse 16

2.16

तामसैर् नोभयं किन्तु वृथायुः-क्षपणं भवेत्। अत्राहं-प्रत्ययी कर्तेत्येवं लोक-व्यवस्थितिः॥

Literal translation

From tamasic states, neither [merit nor demerit] results; rather, life would be wasted in vain. Here, the one with the “I”-notion is the doer; this is how worldly order is arranged.

Word-for-word
तामसैः from tamasic states
न not
उभयम् either [merit or demerit]
किन्तु but
वृथा in vain
आयुः life
क्षपणम् wasting
भवेत् would be
अत्र here
अहम्-प्रत्ययी having the “I”-notion
कर्ता doer
इति thus
एवम् in this way
लोक-व्यवस्थितिः worldly order
Expanded source translation

By tāmasa (thoughts) there is neither of these (karma merit or demerit), rather there would only be spending life’s energy idly. Among these (thoughts of the mind), any one that also includes a notion of ‘I’ (ahaṃ-pratyayin, such as ‘My non-attachment’, ‘I am desirous’, etc.) is called the kartā (the doer, doership). Thus, is our worldly experience (of how the mind reacts through its constituent nature).

स्पष्ट-शब्दादि-युक्तेषु भौतिकत्वम् अतिस्फुटम्। अक्षादावपि तत्-शास्त्र-युक्तिभ्याम् अवधार्यताम्॥

Literal translation

The elemental nature is very clear in things that have clear sound and the rest. Even for the senses and the rest, it should be ascertained through scripture and reasoning.

Word-for-word
स्पष्ट clear
शब्द-आदि sound and the rest
युक्तेषु in things joined with
भौतिकत्वम् elemental nature
अति-स्फुटम् very clear
अक्ष-आदौ in the senses and the rest
अपि also
तत् that
शास्त्र-युक्तिभ्याम् through scripture and reasoning
अवधार्यताम् should be ascertained
Expanded source translation

Concerning these (sense experiences via the thoughts of the mind) consisting of sound, etc., the nature of their also being only products of the (five subtle) elements (bhautikatva) is not clearly known (due to their subtility (saukṣmya, , as well as due to our identification with the mind and senses that we don’t recognize them as objects also). However, even in regard to the senses, etc. (mind, intellect, ego), there is ascertainment (of their elemental nature) through the scripture (śāstra) and (supporting) logic (yukti) on this topic.

Chapter 2 · Verse 18

2.18

एकादशेन्द्रियैर् युक्त्या शास्त्रेणाप्यवगम्यते। यावत् किंचिद् भवेद् एतद् इदं-शब्दोदितं जगत्॥

Literal translation

Whatever in this world is called “this” is understood through the eleven organs, reasoning, and scripture.

Word-for-word
एकादश-इन्द्रियैः through the eleven organs
युक्त्या through reasoning
शास्त्रेण through scripture
अपि also
अवगम्यते is understood
यावत् whatever
किञ्चित् anything
भवेत् may be
एतत् this
इदम्-शब्द-उदितम् called by the word “this”
जगत् world
Expanded source translation

Whatever is experienced through the eleven organs (of the five senses, of the five actions, and the one internal organ), plus that understood through logic and the scripture (as the third separate pramāṇa, means of knowledge, (Yoga Sūtras)), is this world referred to as idam (‘this’, in the following quote).

Chapter 2 · Verse 19

2.19

इदं सर्वं पुरा सृष्टेर् एकम् एवाद्वितीयकम्। सद् एवासीन् नाम-रूपे नास्ताम् इत्यारुणेर् वचः॥

Literal translation

Before creation, all this was Existence alone, one, and without a second. Name and form were not. This is the statement of Āruṇi.

Word-for-word
इदम् this
सर्वम् all
पुरा before
सृष्टेः creation
एकम् one
एव alone
अद्वितीयकम् without a second
सत् Existence
एव alone
आसीत् was
नाम-रूपे name and form
न not
आस्ताम् were
इति thus
आरुणेः of Āruṇi
वचः statement
Expanded source translation

Uddālaka Āruṇi taught (to Śvetaketu, in the sixth chapter of Chāndogya Upaniṣad, , (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)) that before all “this” (idam) manifest universe (śṛṣṭi) “there was one reality only without a second” (ekam eva sad eva a-dvitīyam āsīt); there was no “name or form” (nāma-rūpa).

Chapter 2 · Verse 20

2.20

वृक्षस्य स्वगतो भेदः पत्र-पुष्प-फलादिभिः। वृक्षान्तरात् सजातीयो विजातीयः शिलादितः॥

Literal translation

A tree’s difference within itself is through leaves, flowers, fruits, and the like; from another tree it differs as one of the same kind, and from a stone and the like as a different kind.

Word-for-word
वृक्षस्य of a tree
स्व-गतः within itself
भेदः difference
पत्र leaves
पुष्प flowers
फल fruits
आदिभिः and the like
वृक्ष-अन्तरात् from another tree
स-जातीयः of the same kind
वि-जातीयः of a different kind
शिला-आदितः from a stone and the like
Expanded source translation

A difference (bheda, to make a second, dvitīya, a separate name and form) is (of three types): sva-gata (present within itself), such as of a tree by its leaves, flowers, fruits, etc.; sa-jātīya (between its same class), such as (of one tree) from another tree; and vi-jātīya (apart from another class), such as (of a tree) from a rock, etc.

Chapter 2 · Verse 21

2.21

तथा सद्-वस्तुनो भेद-त्रयं प्राप्तं निवार्यते। ऐक्यावधारण-द्वैत-प्रतिषेधैस् त्रिभिः क्रमात्॥

Literal translation

In the same way, the three differences that might apply to Being are removed in order by the three: oneness, restriction, and denial of duality.

Word-for-word
तथा in the same way
सत्-वस्तुनः of the real existent
भेद-त्रयम् three differences
प्राप्तम् that might apply
निवार्यते is removed
ऐक्य oneness
अवधारण restriction
द्वैत-प्रतिषेधैः by denial of duality
त्रिभिः by three
क्रमात् in order
Expanded source translation

In that way, the prospect that this entity called sat (reality itself) has any of these three differences (from within, between, and apart) is warded off in order by the three (words “one only without-a-second”: eka, eva, a-dvitīya, ) which express oneness (aikya, ‘eka’, no differentiation within itself), restriction (avadhāraṇa, ‘eva’, no differentiation from a similar), and denial of a second thing (dvaita-pratiṣedha, ‘a-dvitīya’, no differentiation from a dissimilar).

Chapter 2 · Verse 22

2.22

सतो नावयवाः शङ्क्यास् तद्-अंशस्यानिरूपणात्। नाम-रूपे न तस्यांशौ तयोर् अद्याप्यनुद्भवात्॥

Literal translation

No parts of Being are to be assumed, because its parts cannot be established. Name and form are not its two parts, because those two have not yet arisen.

Word-for-word
सतः of Being
न not
अवयवाः parts
शङ्क्याः to be assumed
तत्-अंशस्य of parts of that
अनिरूपणात् because they cannot be established
नाम-रूपे name and form
न not
तस्य of it
अंशौ two parts
तयोः of those two
अद्य-अपि even yet
अनुद्भवात् because they have not arisen
Expanded source translation

That reality (sat, brahman) could not possibly have had parts, since there was no discerning of such parts. Names and forms (nāma-rūpa) are not its parts, since before those (names and forms, before this manifest universe those) had not yet arisen.

Chapter 2 · Verse 23

2.23

नाम-रूपोद्भवस्यैव सृष्टित्वात् सृष्टितः पुरा। न तयोरुद्भवस्तस्मात् सन्निरंशं यथा वियत्॥

Literal translation

Because creation is only the arising of name and form, those two had not arisen before creation. Therefore Being is partless, like space.

Word-for-word
नाम-रूप-उद्भवस्य of the arising of name and form
एव only
सृष्टित्वात् because it is creation
सृष्टितः before creation
पुरा before
न not
तयोः of those two
उद्भवः arising
तस्मात् therefore
सत् Being
निरंशम् partless
यथा like
वियत् space
Expanded source translation

Since manifestation is only the arising of names and forms, then before manifestation these two would not have yet arisen. Therefore, this reality (before creation) was partless, just like space (at the start of manifestation, before the other great elements).

Chapter 2 · Verse 24

2.24

सद्-अन्तरं सजातीयं न वैलक्षण्य-वर्जनात्। नाम-रूपोपाधि-भेदं विना नैव सतो भिदा॥

Literal translation

There is no other Being of the same kind, because it has no distinguishing feature. Without the distinction of name and form as limiting adjuncts, Being has no division.

Word-for-word
सत्-अन्तरम् another Being
स-जातीयम् of the same kind
न not
वैलक्षण्य-वर्जनात् because difference is absent
नाम-रूप-उपाधि-भेदम् distinction of name and form as limiting adjuncts
विना without
न not
एव indeed
सतः of Being
भिदा division
Expanded source translation

Since differentiation (vailakṣaṇya) was lacking, there could have been no similarity (sa-jātīya) with another reality (i.e., a class of the same kind of realities). Difference (bheda) is due to the upādhi (limiting adjunct) of names and forms. Without (those), reality cannot have a difference (to be multiple realities).

Chapter 2 · Verse 25

2.25

विजातीयम् असत् तत् तु न खल्वस्तीति गम्यते। नास्यातः प्रतियोगित्वं विजातीयाद् भिदा कुतः॥

Literal translation

Non-being does not exist as something of a different kind. It is understood that it is no opposite of Being; how, then, could there be a difference of another kind?

Word-for-word
वि-जातीयम् of a different kind
असत् non-being
तत् that
तु but
न not
खलु indeed
अस्ति exists
इति thus
गम्यते is understood
न not
अस्य of this
अतः therefore
प्रतियोगित्वम् opposite status
वि-जातीयात् from a different kind
भिदा difference
कुतः how
Expanded source translation

Nor could one conceive of non-reality (a-sat) as vijātīya (belonging to a different class from reality). Since nothing can have opposition (pratiyogin) from this (reality, i.e., ‘existence’ includes everything that possibly or impossibly was, is, or will be, even the notion that there is a non-existence exists), then how could there be a difference (from reality) as a different class?

Chapter 2 · Verse 26

2.26

एकम् एवाद्वितीयं सत् सिद्धम् अत्र तु केचन। विह्वला असद् एवेदं पुरासीद् इत्यावर्णयन्॥

Literal translation

Being is established as one alone, without a second. But some, bewildered, describe this as: “Before, this was non-being alone.”

Word-for-word
एकम् one
एव alone
अद्वितीयम् without a second
सत् Being
सिद्धम् established
अत्र here
तु but
केचन some
विह्वलाः bewildered
असत् non-being
एव alone
इदम् this
पुरा before

Expanded source translation

That reality (sat) is one only without a second has been established. But, in regard to this, some are confused (vihvalas, vyākulas, such as Vaināśikas, Buddhist Nihilists) choosing to say that there was non-reality (a-sat, non-existence) before (the manifestation of the universe).

Chapter 2 · Verse 27

2.27

मग्नस्याब्धौ यथाक्षाणि विह्वलानि तथास्य धीः। अखण्डैक-रसं श्रुत्वा निष्प्रचारा बिभेत्यतः॥

Literal translation

Just as the senses of one sunk in the ocean are bewildered, so his mind, on hearing of the one undivided essence, becomes inactive and is afraid.

Word-for-word
मग्नस्य of one sunk
अब्धौ in the ocean
यथा just as
अक्षाणि the senses
विह्वलानि bewildered
तथा so
अस्य his
धीः mind
अखण्ड-एक-रसम् the one undivided essence
श्रुत्वा on hearing

अतः therefore
Expanded source translation

Like sinking into the ocean (with nothing but water all around) one’s senses and mind are bewildered, upon hearing that reality is one without divisions (to cling to). These individuals have thus become stunned and very fearful.

Chapter 2 · Verse 28

2.28

गौडाचार्या निर्विकल्पे समाधावन्य-योगिनाम्। साकार-ध्यान-निष्ठानाम् अत्यन्तं भयमूचिरे॥

Literal translation

The Gauḍācārya spoke of great fear among other yogis devoted to meditation on form, in non-conceptual samādhi.

Word-for-word
गौडाचार्या Gauḍācārya [the teacher]
निर्विकल्पे in non-conceptual
समाधौ samādhi
अन्य-योगिनाम् of other yogis
साकार-ध्यान-निष्ठानाम् devoted to meditation on form
अत्यन्तम् great

The teacher Gauḍa-pāda talked about the great fear of some yogins ( (Māṇḍūkya Up. Kārikā)) who are dedicated only to brahman with a form (sākāra) when their contemplation becomes free of (mental) divisions.

Chapter 2 · Verse 29

2.29

अस्पर्श-योगो नामैष दुर्दर्शः सर्व-योगिभिः। योगिनो बिभ्यति ह्य्-अस्माद् अभये भय-दर्शिनः॥

Literal translation

This is called asparśa-yoga; it is hard for all yogis to perceive. Indeed, yogis fear it, seeing fear in the fearless.

Word-for-word
अस्पर्श-योगः asparśa-yoga
नाम by name
एषः this
दुर्दर्शः hard to perceive
सर्व-योगिभिः by all yogis
योगिनः yogis
बिभ्यति are afraid
हि indeed

All such yogins, who find what is called a-sparśa (without a sense or mental contact) yoga difficult to conceive, are afraid of it, seeing fear in the fearless.

Chapter 2 · Verse 30

2.30

भगवत्-पूज्य-पादाश्च शुष्क-तर्क-पटून् अमून्। आहुर् माध्यमिकान् भ्रान्तान् अचिन्त्येऽस्मिन् सद्-आत्मनि॥

Literal translation

Bhagavatpāda calls these Mādhyamikas, skilled in dry reasoning, confused about this inconceivable true Self.

Word-for-word
भगवत्-पूज्य-पादाः Bhagavatpāda, the revered teacher
च and
शुष्क-तर्क-पटून् skilled in dry reasoning
अमून् these
आहुः call
माध्यमिकान् Mādhyamikas
भ्रान्तान् confused
अचिन्त्ये in the inconceivable
अस्मिन् this
सत्-आत्मनि real Self
Expanded source translation

The highly respected Bhagavat-pāda (Śaṅkara) calls the Mādhyamikas (Buddhists) who only have dry logic (lacking the Veda as the proper means of knowledge here) as confused regarding this reality-self which (as the witness) cannot be an object of thought.

Chapter 2 · Verse 31

2.31

अनादृत्य श्रुतिं मौर्ख्याद् इमे बौद्धास्तपस्विनः। आपेदिरे निरात्मत्वम् अनुमानैक-चक्षुषः॥

Literal translation

These Buddhist ascetics, through confusion, disregarded śruti and reached the view that there is no Self, seeing through inference alone.

Word-for-word
अनादृत्य having disregarded
श्रुतिम् śruti
मौर्ख्यात् through confusion
इमे these
बौद्धाः Buddhists
तपस्विनः ascetics
आपेदिरे reached
निरात्मत्वम् the view that there is no Self
अनुमान-एक-चक्षुषः having inference as their only eye
Expanded source translation

These Buddhists, (seemly) out of dumbness (lack of a proper means of knowledge here) disregard the scripture (śruti, teachings) and remain in darkness. As they only look through logic, they arrive at the conclusion that they themselves are nothing (nir-ātmatva).

Chapter 2 · Verse 32

2.32

शून्यम् आसीद् इति ब्रूषे सद्-योगं वा सद्-आत्मताम्। शून्यस्य न तु तद्-युक्तम् उभयं व्याहतत्वतः॥

Literal translation

You say, “Nothing was.” Do you mean that nothing is joined to Being, or that it is Being? Neither claim fits nothingness, because both are contradictory.

Word-for-word
शून्यम् nothingness
आसीत् was
इति thus
ब्रूषे you say
सत्-योगम् connection with Being
वा or
सत्-आत्मताम् being Being
शून्यस्य of nothingness
न not
तु but
तत् that
युक्तम् fitting
उभयम् both
व्याहतत्वतः because they are contradictory
Expanded source translation

When you (Buddhists) say śūnya (nothingness) existed, did you mean that it has existence (sat-yoga) or that it is existence (sat-ātmatā)? In either case, nothingness cannot have any such association with existence, because both non-existence and existence are contradictory (to each other, but if they mean the same thing to you then you are simply naming existence as ‘śūnya’).

Chapter 2 · Verse 33

2.33

न युक्तस् तमसा सूर्यो नापि चासौ तमोमयः। सच्-छून्ययोर् विरोधित्वाच् छून्यम् आसीत् कथं वद॥

Literal translation

The sun is not joined with darkness, nor is it made of darkness. Since Being and non-being are opposed, how can you say that non-being was?

Word-for-word
न not
युक्तः joined
तमसा with darkness
सूर्यः the sun
न not
अपि also
च and
असौ that
तमो-मयः made of darkness
सत्-शून्ययोः of Being and non-being
विरोधित्वात् because of opposition
शून्यम् non-being
आसीत् was
कथम् how
वद say
Expanded source translation

The sun cannot be attributed with darkness, nor does it consist of darkness. As existence and non-existence are (naturally) contradictory, how could you say non-existence existed (before creation)?

Chapter 2 · Verse 34

2.34

वियद्-आदेर् नाम-रूपे मायया सुविकल्पिते। शून्यस्य नाम-रूपे च तथा चेज् जीव्यतां चिरम्॥

Literal translation

Name and form beginning with space are imagined in Being by māyā. If name and form are likewise [imagined] in nothingness, then live long!

Word-for-word
वियत्-आदेः beginning with space
नाम-रूपे name and form
मायया by māyā
सति in Being
कल्पिते are imagined
शून्यस्य of nothingness
नाम-रूपे name and form
च also
तथा in the same way
चेत् if
जीव्यताम् let [you] live
चिरम् long
Expanded source translation

(The Buddhist says:) If (for you Vedāntins) the names and forms beginning with the element space, etcetera are completely imposed (on existence) by (the inexplicable magic of) māyā, then similarly (for us Buddhists) these are simply names and forms of non-existence (śūnya, imposed, produced, by māyā). (We reply:) May you live long! (i.e., you either are talking meaninglessly or at best not disputing us, since you are accepting a thing called ‘śūnya’ that has names and forms imposed on it).

Chapter 2 · Verse 35

2.35

सतोऽपि नाम-रूपे द्वे कल्पिते चेत् तदा वद। कुत्रेति निरधिष्ठानो न भ्रमः क्वचित् ईक्ष्यते॥

Literal translation

If name and form are imagined even in Being, then say where. An illusion is never seen anywhere without a basis.

Word-for-word
सतः in Being
अपि even
नाम-रूपे name and form
द्वे two
कल्पिते are imagined
चेत् if
तदा then
वद say
कुत्र where
इति thus
निरधिष्ठानः without a basis
न not
भ्रमः an illusion
क्वचित् anywhere
ईक्ष्यते is seen
Expanded source translation

You may say that both names and forms of reality are both imposed (by māyā upon non-existence), but an illusion (bhrama) is never seen anywhere without a substratum (e.g., mirage water requires a certain surface condition viewed at a certain angle; a phantom snake requires a crack on the ground, a rope, etc. in a darkened area by one who would suspect a snake could be there).

Chapter 2 · Verse 36

2.36

सद् आसीद् इति शब्दार्थ-भेदे वैगुण्यम् आपतेत्। अभेदे पुनर् उक्तिः स्यान् मैवं लोके तथेक्षणात्॥

Literal translation

If the words “Being” and “was” have different meanings, a defect follows. If they have the same meaning, it would be repetition. Do not say this, for such usage is seen in the world.

Word-for-word
सत् Being
आसीत् was
इति thus
शब्द-अर्थ-भेदे if the word and meaning differ
वैगुण्यम् a defect
आपतेत् would follow
अभेदे if there is no difference
पुनः again
उक्तिः repetition
स्यात् would be
मा do not
एवम् so
लोके in the world
तथा such
ईक्षणात् because it is seen
Expanded source translation

(Objection:) The (Veda text’s) two words ‘sat’ ‘āsīt’ (‘reality was’) either separately refer to two different entities (śabdārthas, hence there is duality), or the expression refers to no difference (a-bheda, and hence is meaningless tautology, like ‘one is one’). (Reply:) It should not be like that, since we see such expressions in common usage.

Chapter 2 · Verse 37

2.37

कर्तव्यं कुरुते वाक्यं ब्रूते धार्यस्य धारणम्। इत्यादि-वासनाविष्टं प्रत्यासीत् सद् इतीरणम्॥

Literal translation

“One does what must be done,” “one speaks,” and “one carries what must be carried”: for someone filled with habits of such speech, the expression “Being was” is familiar.

Word-for-word
कर्तव्यम् what must be done
कुरुते one does
वाक्यम् a word
ब्रूते one speaks
धार्यस्य what must be carried
धारणम् carrying
इति-आदि and so on
वासन-अविष्टम् filled with habits
प्रत्यासीत् is familiar to one nearby
सत्-इति “Being”
ईरणम् the expression
Expanded source translation

‘A deed is done,’ ‘A speech is spoken,’ ‘A burden is borne’ – towards one who is accustomed to such expressions, the verb ‘was’ (in ‘sat āsīt’) expresses being (sat).

Chapter 2 · Verse 38

2.38

कालाभावे पुरेत्युक्तिः काल-वासनया युतम्। शिष्यं प्रत्येव तेनात्र द्वितीयं नहि शङ्क्यते॥

Literal translation

The word “before,” where there is no time, is used for the student who has a habit of time; therefore no second thing is to be suspected here.

Word-for-word
काल-अभावे where there is no time
पुरा before
इति thus
उक्तिः the expression
काल-वासनया with a habit of time
युतम् endowed
शिष्यम् the student

अत्र here

न not

शङ्क्यते is to be suspected
Expanded source translation

The expression ‘before’ (purā, agre) in regard to (‘before creation’) which lacks time is directed toward a student accustomed to temporal thinking, and this usage (by the teacher) here does not intend duality (existence plus time).

Chapter 2 · Verse 39

2.39

चोद्यं वा परिहारो वा क्रियतां द्वैत-भाषया। अद्वैत-भाषया चोद्यं नास्ति नापि तद्-उत्तरम्॥

Literal translation

Let a question or its answer be made in dualistic speech. In non-dual speech there is no question, nor its answer.

Word-for-word
चोद्यम् a question
वा or
परिहारः an answer
वा or
क्रियताम् let it be made
द्वैत-भाषया in dualistic speech
अद्वैत-भाषया in non-dual speech
चोद्यम् a question
न not
अस्ति exists
न not
अपि also
तत्-उत्तरम् an answer to it
Expanded source translation

A question (codya, pūrva-pakṣa) and its reply arise within our duality accustomed language (within nāma-rūpa, names and forms). Within a (supposed) non-duality (or non-existent) language, there can be no question or its response.

Chapter 2 · Verse 40

2.40

तदा स्तिमित-गम्भीरं न तेजो न तमस्ततम्। अनाख्यम् अनभिव्यक्तं सत् किञ्चिद् अवशिष्यते॥

Literal translation

Then, still and deep, with neither light nor darkness spread out, some nameless, unmanifest Being remains.

Word-for-word
तदा then
स्तिमित still
गम्भीरम् deep
न not
तेजः light
न not
तमः darkness
ततम् spread out
अनाख्यम् nameless
अनभिव्यक्तम् unmanifest
सत् Being
किञ्चित् some
अवशिष्यते remains
Expanded source translation

At that time (before creation) a ‘steady depth’ (‘gambhīra’,* a-dvaita vastu) pervaded without any tejas or tamas (opposition guṇas, light-dark, movement-stasis), nor name or manifest form apart from this reality (sat). Non-being then existed not nor being: There was no air, nor sky that is beyond it. What was concealed? Wherein? In whose protection? And was there deep (gambhīra) unfathomable water?(1) Death then existed not nor life immortal; Of neither night nor day was any token. By its inherent force the One breathed windless: No other thing than that beyond existed.(2) Darkness there was at first by darkness hidden; Without distinctive marks, this all was water. That which, becoming, by the void was covered. That One by force of heat came into being.(3) Desire entered the One in the beginning: It was the earliest seed, of thought the product. The sages searching in their hearts with wisdom, Found out the bond of being in non-being.(4) Their ray extended light across the darkness: But was the One above or was it under? Creative force was there, and fertile power: Below was energy, above was impulse.(5) Who knows for certain? Who shall here declare it? Whence was it born, and whence came this creation? The gods were born after this world's creation: Then who can know from whence it has arisen?(6) None knows whence creation has arisen; And whether he has or has not produced it: He who surveys it in the highest heaven, He only knows, or haply he may know not.(7)

Chapter 2 · Verse 41

2.41

ननु भूम्यादिकं मा भूत् परमाण्वन्त-नाशतः। कथं ते वियतोऽसत्त्वं बुद्धिम् आरोहतीति चेत्॥

Literal translation

“Let earth and the rest be absent, dissolved down to atoms. How can the non-being of space enter your understanding?”—if this is asked.

Word-for-word
ननु but / if it is said
भूमि-आदिकम् earth and the rest
मा let not
भूत् be
परमाणु-अन्त-नाशतः because of dissolution down to atoms
कथम् how
ते your
वियतः of space
असत्त्वम् non-being
बुद्धिम् understanding
आरोहति enters
इति thus
चेत् if
Expanded source translation

Question (nanu): Upon dissolution all the way to the atomic elements (paramāṇus) then the earth, etcetera may cease to exist, but how can I arrive at a notion that space (ākāśa) itself has no existence?

Chapter 2 · Verse 42

2.42

अत्यन्तं निर्जगद् व्योम यथा ते बुद्धिम् आश्रितम्। तथैव सन् निराकाशं कुतो नाश्रयते मतिम्॥

Literal translation

Just as space completely without a world is accepted in your understanding, so why does Being without space not take hold of the mind?

Word-for-word
अत्यन्तम् completely
निर्-जगत् without a world
व्योम space
यथा just as
ते your
बुद्धिम् understanding
आश्रितम् is accepted
तथा so
एव indeed

निर्-आकाशम् without space

न not

मतिम् of the mind
Expanded source translation

If in fact you can have such an abiding knowledge that there is a space completely without a universe (of names and forms), then why can't you abide in a idea that reality (sat) can be without space?

Chapter 2 · Verse 43

2.43

निर्जगद् व्योम दृष्टं चेत् प्रकाश-तमसी विना। क्व दृष्टं किंच ते पक्षे न प्रत्यक्षं वियत् खलु॥

Literal translation

If space without a world is seen apart from light and darkness, where is it seen? And in your view, space itself is not directly perceived.

Word-for-word
निर्-जगत् without a world
व्योम space
दृष्टम् seen
चेत् if
प्रकाश-तमसी light and darkness
विना without
क्व where
दृष्टम् is it seen
किञ्च and
ते in your

प्रत्यक्षम् directly perceived
वियत् space
खलु indeed
Expanded source translation

If you can perceive a space without a universe, then in that case, without (the contrast of) light and dark, where could you possibly perceive (a universe-less space)? Moreover, space is indeed unseen (na pratyakṣa, is not in fact an object of the eye).

Chapter 2 · Verse 44

2.44

सद् वस्तु शुद्धं त्वस्माभिर् निश्चितैर् अनुभूयते। तूष्णीं स्थितौ न शून्यत्वं शून्य-बुद्धेश्च वर्जनात्॥

Literal translation

The pure reality of Being is experienced by us who are certain. When [the mind] is quiet, it is not nothingness, because the thought of nothingness is absent.

Word-for-word
सत् Being
वस्तु reality
शुद्धम् pure
तु indeed
अस्माभिः by us
निश्चितैः who are certain
अनुभूयते is experienced
तूष्णीम् quietly
स्थितौ in the state
न not
शून्यत्वम् nothingness
शून्य-बुद्धेः of the thought of nothingness
च and
वर्जनात् because of absence
Expanded source translation

Whereas, reality (sat, brahman) is pure existence (vastu) experienced (anu-bhūyate, literally ‘being in keeping with’) by all of us very clearly. When (the mind) remains quiet, we do not experience nothing, because there is no thought of a nothing (śūnya, at that time).

Chapter 2 · Verse 45

2.45

सद्-बुद्धिर् अपि चेन् नास्ति मास्त्वस्य स्व-प्रभत्वतः। निर्मनस्कत्व-साक्षित्वात् सन्-मात्रं सुगमं नृणाम्॥

Literal translation

Even if the thought of Being is absent, let it be absent, because Being is self-luminous. Because it witnesses the absence of mind, mere Being is easy for people [to know].

Word-for-word
सत्-बुद्धिः thought of Being
अपि even
चेत् if
न not
अस्ति exists
मा let not
अस्तु be
अस्य of this
स्व-प्रभत्वतः because of self-luminosity
निर्मनस्कत्व absence of mind
साक्षित्वात् because of being the witness
सत्-मात्रम् mere Being
सुगमम् easy to grasp
नृणाम् for people
Expanded source translation

(Objection:) But neither do we have a thought of existence (at that quiet time). (Reply:) Let that thought not be there, because existence is self-revealing (sva-prabhatva) and because it is the witness (sākṣitva) of the lack of thoughts (at that time). Pure existence is easy to recognize for everyone (as everyone is effortlessly always shining and witnessing whatever is there or not in their mind – a quiet mind is just an aid to confirm this teaching that it is you alone who is shining and witnessing, not any of these objects witnessed).

Chapter 2 · Verse 46

2.46

मनो-जृम्भण-राहिते यथा साक्षी निराकुलः। माया-जृम्भणतः पूर्वं सत् तथैव निराकुलम्॥

When the mind is not opening up (to an external world) then the witness (the existence of oneself) appears to be without problems (nir-ākula). Similarly (as it is now, so it was then), before the opening up (of the universe by) māyā, reality (sat) was unruffled.

Chapter 2 · Verse 47

2.47

निस्तत्वा कार्य-गम्यास्य शक्तिर् मायाऽग्नि-शक्तिवत्। न हि शक्तिः क्वचित् कैश्चिद् बुध्यते कार्यतः पुरा॥

Apart (nis-ta-tvā, pṛthak) from manifesting its effects, māyā is (only inferred to exist within reality as) a śakti (power, to manifest the varieties of nature from the one reality), like the power of fire (to burn only is known by its perceived effects). Because, no one knows any power exists somewhere, before its effects (are noticed).

Chapter 2 · Verse 48

2.48

न सद्-वस्तु सतः शक्तिर् न हि वह्नेः स्व-शक्तिता। सद्-विलक्षणतायां तु शक्तेर् किं तत्त्वम् उच्यताम्॥

The power (śakti, māyā) of reality is not the reality itself. Nor can a power exist by itself (like) fire’s (power to burn does not exist apart from fire itself). If (this power, māyā) exists apart from reality, what could one say is its nature?

Chapter 2 · Verse 49

2.49

शून्यत्वम् इति चेच् छून्यं माया-कार्यम् इतीरितम्। न शून्यं नापि सद् यादृक् तादृक् तत्वम् इहेष्यताम्॥

If (you say the power, māyā) is the nature of non-existence (śūnyatva), (then this contradicts) what you said before that it is an effect of māyā (). (Māyā) is neither non-existence (śūnya) nor reality itself (sat) – whatever that is (yādṛk, neither sat nor a-sat), that (tādṛk) has to be considered its (māyā’s) nature (tatva = tattva, (Sanskrit Grammar)).

Chapter 2 · Verse 50

2.50

नासद् आसीन् नो सद् आसीत् तदानीं किंत्वभूत् तमः। सद्-योगात् तमसः सत्त्वं न स्वतस् तन्-निषेधनात्॥

(Hence it was said in Ṛg Veda, ) There was neither a-sat nor sat at that time (before creation), but there was tamas (darkness, which was what māyā is before creation, ). Existence (‘was’) is attributed to tamas (that darkness) due to its association with (i.e., appearance within) existence (sat), not due to itself alone, since (existence) is denied to it (in that Ṛg Veda hymn).

Chapter 2 · Verse 51

2.51

अत एव द्वितीयतं शून्यवन् न हि गण्यते। न लोके चैत्र-तच्-छक्त्योर् जीवितं लिख्यते पृथक्॥

Thus, like śūnya, (māyā) cannot count as a second entity (from existence, sat). In the world, an able person and his ability cannot be portrayed to live apart from each other.

Chapter 2 · Verse 52

2.52

शक्त्याधिक्ये जीवितं चेत् वर्धते तत्र वृद्धि-कृत्। न शक्तिः किन्तु तत्-कार्यं युद्ध-कृष्यादिकं तथा॥

If one’s life lengthens when one’s power increases, in that case, the act of ageing is not itself the power (to live, one’s prāṇa) but an effect of that power, such as making war or going agriculture, etcetera (are possible effects of one’s power to live). (Similarly, although māyā, the manifestation power of existence, is not an addition to that sat, the universe consists of separate effects, which do vary, of that non-addition māyā.)

Chapter 2 · Verse 53

2.53

सर्वथा शक्ति-मात्रस्य न पृथक् गणना क्वचित्। शक्ति-कार्यं तु नैवास्ति द्वितीयं शङ्क्यते कथम्॥

Everywhere, a śakti (any subtle power) itself cannot count as being separate (from that existence, or whether an element, a person or the Lord) in which it manifests, and any effect of that śakti is not itself (the śakti). How could it act as a power separately (from where it manifests)?

Chapter 2 · Verse 54

2.54

न कृस्त्न-ब्रह्म-वृत्तिः सा शक्तिः किंत्वेक-देश-भाक्। घट-शक्तिर् यथा भूमौ स्निग्ध-मृद्येव वर्तते॥

This power (of brahman, reality) does not operate everywhere throughout brahman, but rather only occurs in some part (of existence). Just as the power in earth to (materially) produce clay pots only occurs in softened clay, not elsewhere.

Chapter 2 · Verse 55

2.55

पादोऽस्य सर्वा भूतानि त्रि-पाद् अस्ति स्वयं-प्रभः। इत्येक-देश-वृत्तित्वं मायया वदति श्रुतिः॥

“Everything (the effects of māyā, manifest to our senses and mind) is only one quarter of this (reality), the other three quarters…” ( (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)) are only this one self-revealing (svayaṃ-prabha, sat). Thus, the scripture reveals māyā as being only a portion (of reality).

Chapter 2 · Verse 56

2.56

विष्टभ्याहम् इदं कृत्स्नम् एकांशेन स्थितो जगत्। इति कृष्णोऽर्जुनायाह जगतस् त्वेक-देशताम्॥

“I remain sustaining this entire universe with (just) a fraction (of My self)” ( (Bhagavad Gītā)). Thus, Lord Kṛṣṇa indicates to Arjuna the fractional nature of the universe.

Chapter 2 · Verse 57

2.57

स भूमिं विश्वतो वृत्वा ह्यत्यतिष्ठद् दशाङ्गुलम्। विकारावर्ति चात्रास्ति श्रुति-सूत्र-कृतोर् वचः॥

“This one envelops the entire universe, yet extends beyond by ten fingers” (i.e., innumerably, beyond what is the limit of the perceivable, Ṛg Veda 10.129 & (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad)); and “(Brahman) is without form (vikāra-avartin, not needing a form) here (beyond the universe of forms)” ( (Brahma Sūtras)) – thus is the declaration made in scripture (śruti) and in the teaching aphorisms (sūtras).

Chapter 2 · Verse 58

2.58

निरंशेऽप्यंशम् आरोप्य कृत्स्नेंऽशे वेति पृच्छतः। तद्-भाषयोत्तरं ब्रूते श्रुतिः श्रोतृ-हितैषिणी॥

Attributing (āropya) parts even upon the partless (sat), the śruti, for the benefit of the listener (who is still bound up in duality), answers with the same language of the question as to whether (māyā pervades) completely or only part (of reality).

Chapter 2 · Verse 59

2.59

सत्-तत्त्वम् आश्रिता शक्तिः कल्पयेत् सति विक्रियाः। वर्णा भित्ति-गता भित्तौ चित्रं नाना-विधं तथा॥

Śakti (this māyā) whose truth is reality (sat-tattva) creates (kalpyayet, conjures as if by magic) differences in reality (the non-dual sat), like paints applied to a wall appear as (if a realistic, 3-D) complex painting on the wall.

Chapter 2 · Verse 60

2.60

आद्यो विकार आकाशः सोऽवकाश-स्वरूपवान्। आकाशोऽस्तीति सत्-तत्त्वम् आकाशेऽप्यनुगच्छति॥

The first modification (the first of the five great elements from māyā) was ākāśa (space). Space is that which gives room (avakāśa, provides dimension). (Being a modification of māyā) its truth also is only (the non-dual) reality (sat-tattva).

Chapter 2 · Verse 61

2.61

एक-स्वभावं सत्-तत्त्वम् आकाशो द्वि-स्वभावकः। नावकाशः सति व्योम्नि स चैषोऽपि द्वयं स्थितम्॥

The nature of reality (sat-tattva) is only its own single nature (as existence itself). Space has two natures (as dimension and as existing). In existence itself there is no dimension. In space there is also that (dimension), and thus is dual.

Chapter 2 · Verse 62

2.62

यद्वा प्रतिध्वनिर् व्योम्नो गुणो नासौ सतीक्ष्यते। व्योम्नि द्वौ सद् ध्वनी तेन सद् एकं द्वि-गुणं वियत्॥

Also sound (pratidhvani, perceptible by the sense of hearing) is a quality (guṇa) of space, but this (quality) is not perceived in reality itself. In space there are both sound and existence. So existence is a single (nature) and space is dual natured (dvi-guṇa)*. *(Here, although existence is the very nature of space, it is lumped in as another guṇa based on the common notion of people regarding ‘existence’ that it is merely an attribute which can be there or not be there, as in “the pot ‘is’”, or “the pot ‘is not’”, ).

Chapter 2 · Verse 63

2.63

या शक्तिः कल्पयेद् व्योम सा सद्-व्योम्नोर् अभिन्नताम्। आपाद्य धर्म-धर्मित्वं व्यत्ययेनावकल्पयेत्॥

The same śakti (māyā) that produces space, first produces the notion that existence and space are inseparable (that space exists) and then conjures up the opposite notion that the two are related as a quality and its possessor (dharma-dharmitva, that space has existence or existence has space).

Chapter 2 · Verse 64

2.64

सतो व्योमत्वम् आपन्नं व्योम्नः सत्तां तु लौकिकाः। तार्किकाश्चावगच्छन्ति मायाया उचितं हि तत्॥

It is existence that (initially) appears (by māyā) to have the nature of space (sataḥ vyomatvam, like clay has clay-potness). But logicians (tārkikas), from their worldly perspective (laukikas), then think instead that space has the nature of existence (vyomnaḥ sattām, that ‘space exists’ means space is an independent reality). That indeed would be expected due to māyā (the power of projection, which can conjure up unreal relationships).

Chapter 2 · Verse 65

2.65

यद् यथा वर्तते तस्य तथात्वं भाति मानतः। अन्यथात्वं भ्रमेणेति न्यायोऽयं सार्व-लौकिकः॥

It is common knowledge by a proper means of knowledge (mānataḥ, pratyakṣādi-pramāṇataḥ) that a thing appears as it is (i.e., tasmin tad-buddhiḥ), and to be otherwise (anyathātva) would be by error (bhrama, an illusion).

Chapter 2 · Verse 66

2.66

एवं श्रुति-विचारात् प्राग् यथा यद् वस्तु भासते। विचारेण विपर्येति ततस् तच्-चिन्त्यतां वियत्॥

In this way, before inquiry into the scripture (which is here the appropriate means of knowledge, pramāṇa), something appears different afterwards by proper inquiry. Therefore, let us discuss what this space is.

Chapter 2 · Verse 67

2.67

भिन्ने वियत्-सती शब्द-भेदाद् बुद्धेश्च भेदतः। वाय्वादिष्वनुवृत्तं सन् न तु व्योमेति भेद-धीः॥

Space and existence are different because their names (i.e., nāmans) are different and their understandings (i.e., rūpas) are different. Existence encompasses (anuvṛtta) space, but that is not the case for space (which does not encompass existence, i.e., existence was there before the manifestation of space, as well as space is only a ‘part’ of reality). That is their different understanding (bheda-dhī).

Chapter 2 · Verse 68

2.68

सद् वस्त्वधिक-वृत्तित्वाद् धर्मि व्योम्नस् तु धर्मता। धिया सतः पृथक्-कारे ब्रूहि व्योम किम् आत्मकं॥

Existence, because of being completely inclusive (in time and place) of any entity, is the dharmin (the locus or substance of all entities), whereas space has the nature of being a dharma (a seeming attribute of reality, of this locus). By this understanding (dhiyā), once existence itself is distinguished (is abstracted, from space), then space has what kind of nature (if it is other than reality and is imposed by māyā upon reality)?

Chapter 2 · Verse 69

2.69

अवकाशात्मकं तच् चेद् असत् तद् इति चिन्त्यताम्। भिन्नं सतोऽसच् च नेति वक्षि चेद् व्याहतिस् तव॥

If you say that its nature is (not reality but is) whatever gives dimension (avakāśa-ātmaka), then it should be considered to be a-sat (not-real). If you say (vakṣi) that it (space) exists as other than reality yet it is not not-real (not a-sat), then you contradict yourself.

Chapter 2 · Verse 70

2.70

भातीति चेद् भातु नाम भूषणं मायिकस्य तत्। यद् असद् भासमानं तन् मिथ्या स्वप्न-गजादिवत्॥
