Even when on the acquisition of the desired external objects the desire becomes quiescent and the Vṛtti is directed inward, it reflects the bliss of Brahman. (This is what is known as ‘reflected’ bliss or Viṣayānanda or bliss derived from the enjoyment of external things.)

Chapter 11 · Verse 87

11.87

ब्रह्मानन्दो वासना च प्रतिबिम्ब इति त्रयम्। अन्तरेण जगत्यस्मिन्नानन्दो नास्ति कश्चन॥

There are thus only three kinds of bliss experienced in the world: (1) Brahmānanda, the bliss of Brahman; (2) Vāsanānanda, the bliss arising in the quiescent mind out of the impressions of Brahmānanda and (3) Viṣayānanda, the bliss resulting from the fulfilment of the desire to be in contact with external objects.

Chapter 11 · Verse 88

11.88

तथा च विषयानन्दो वासनानन्द इत्यमू। आनन्दौ जनयन्नास्ते ब्रह्मानन्दः स्वयंप्रभः॥

Of these, the self-revealing bliss of Brahman gives rise to the other two kinds of bliss, the Vāsanānanda and the Viṣayānanda.

Chapter 11 · Verse 89

11.89

श्रुतियुक्त्यनुभूतिभ्यः स्वप्रकाशचिदात्मके। ब्रह्मानन्दे सुप्तिकाले सिद्धे सत्यन्यदा शृणु॥

The fact that the bliss of Brahman is self-revealing in deep sleep is established by the authority of the scriptures, by reasoning and by one’s experience. Now hear about its experience at other times.

Chapter 11 · Verse 90

11.90

य आनन्दमयः सुप्तौ स विज्ञानमयात्मताम्। गत्वा स्वप्नं प्रबोधं वा प्राप्नोति स्थानभेदतः॥

The Jīva which is called Ānandamaya, enjoying bliss of Brahman during sleep gets identified with the intellect-sheath during the dreaming and waking states, as he changes his seat from one state to another.

Chapter 11 · Verse 91

11.91

नेत्रे जागरणं कण्ठे स्वप्नः सुप्तिर्हृदम्बुजे। आपादमस्तकं देहं व्याप्य जागर्ति चेतनः॥

The Śruti says that in the waking state the Jīva abides in the eye i.e., the gross body; in the dreaming state in the throat and in deep sleep in the lotus of the heart. In the waking state the Jīva pervades the whole gross body from head to foot.

Chapter 11 · Verse 92

11.92

देहतादात्म्यमापन्नस्तप्तायः पिण्डवत्ततः। अहं मनुष्य इत्येवं निश्चित्यैवावतिष्ठते॥

In the waking state the Jīva gets identified with the body, as fire with a red-hot ball of iron. As a result of this he comes to feel with certainty: ‘I am a man’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 93

11.93

उदासीनः सुखी दुःखीत्यवस्थात्रयमेत्यसौ। सुखदुःखे कर्मकार्ये त्वौदासीन्यं स्वभावतः॥

The Jīva experiences the three states of detachment, joy and suffering. Joy and suffering are the results of actions; detachment comes naturally.

Chapter 11 · Verse 94

11.94

बाह्यभोगान्मनोराज्यात्सुखदुःखे द्विधा मते। सुखदुःखान्तरालेषु भवेत्तूष्णीमवस्थितिः॥

Pain and pleasure are of two sorts as the experience is limited within the mind or is external to it also. The state of detachment appears in the intervals between pain and pleasure.

Chapter 11 · Verse 95

11.95

न कापि चिन्ता मेऽस्त्यद्य सुखमास इति ब्रुवन्। औदासीन्ये निजानन्दभानं वक्त्यखिलः जनः॥

‘Now I have no worries, I am happy’, thus do people describe the natural bliss of the Self in the state of detachment.

Chapter 11 · Verse 96

11.96

अहमस्मीत्यहङ्कारसामान्येनावृतत्वतः। निजानन्दो न मुख्योऽयं किन्त्वसौ तस्य वासना॥

But in this state the natural bliss of the Self is not primary for it is obscured by the idea of egoity and the bliss so experienced is not the bliss of Brahman but only an impression of it.

Chapter 11 · Verse 97

11.97

नीरपूरितभाण्डस्य बाह्ये शैत्यं न तज्जलम्। किन्तु नीरगुणस्तेन नीरसत्तानुमीयते॥

The outside of a pot full of water feels cold. Actually there is no water outside but coldness only. It is from this property of water that the presence of water inside is inferred.

Chapter 11 · Verse 98

11.98

यावद्यावदहङ्कारो विस्मृतोऽभ्यासयोगतः। तावत्तावत्सूक्ष्मदृष्टेर्निजानन्दोऽनुमीयते॥

Similarly, as one forgets one’s egoity by continued practice, one can comprehend through intuitive perception one’s natural state of bliss.

Chapter 11 · Verse 99

11.99

सर्वात्मना विस्मृतः सन्सूक्ष्मतां परमां व्रजेत्। अलीनत्वान्न निद्रैषा ततो देहोऽपि नो पतेत्॥

By continued practice of all kinds the ego becomes exceedingly refined. This state is not sleep because the ego is not completely absorbed; moreover the body does not, as in sleep, fall to the ground.

Chapter 11 · Verse 100

11.100

न द्वैतं भासते नापि निद्रा तत्रास्ति यत्सुखम्। स ब्रह्मानन्द इत्याह भगवानर्जुनं प्रति॥

The bliss in which there is no experience of duality and which is not sleep either, is the bliss of Brahman. So said Lord Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna.

Chapter 11 · Verse 101

11.101

शनैः शनैरुपरमेद्बुद्ध्या धृतिगृहीतया। आत्मसंस्थं मनः कृत्वा न किंचिदपि चिन्तयेत्॥

‘By the steady application of reason and discrimination an aspirant should gradually control his mind. He should keep the mind fixed on the Self and restrain it from thinking of anything else’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 102

11.102

यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम्। ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत्॥

‘Whenever the mind which is restless and fickle, wanders away, the aspirant should restrain it and concentrate it on the Self’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 103

11.103

प्रशान्तमनसं ह्येनं योगिनं सुखमुत्तमम्। उपैति शान्तरजसं ब्रह्मभूतमकल्मषम्॥

‘The Yogī whose mind is perfectly tranquil, whose passions are subdued, who is sinless and has become Brahman, attains the supreme bliss’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 104

11.104

यत्रोपरमते चित्तं निरुद्धं योगसेवया। यत्र चैवात्मनात्मानं पश्यन्नात्मनि तुष्यति॥

‘When by practice of Yoga, his mind is withdrawn and concentrated, the Yogī sees the Self by the Self and finds supreme satisfaction in the Self’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 105

11.105

सुखमात्यन्तिकं यत्तद्बुद्धिग्राह्यमतीन्द्रियम्। वेत्ति यत्र न चैवायं स्थितश्चलति तत्त्वतः॥

‘When he obtains that supreme bliss which is beyond the senses, but which can be grasped by the intellect, he becomes firmly rooted in it and is never moved from it’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 106

11.106

यं लब्ध्वा चापरं लाभं मन्यते नाधिकं ततः। यस्मिन् स्थितो न दुःखेन गुरुणापि विचाल्यते॥

‘Attaining it he considers no other gain as superior. Once established in it he is not disturbed even by great sorrow’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 107

11.107

तं विद्याद्दुःखसंयोगवियोगं योगसंज्ञितम्। स निश्चयेन योक्तव्यो योगोऽनिर्विण्णचेतसा॥

‘This science of separation from the painful association is called Yoga. This Yoga must be practised with faith and a steady and undespairing mind’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 108

11.108

युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगि विगतकल्मषः। सुखेन ब्रह्मसंस्पर्शमत्यन्तं सुखमश्नुते॥

‘A Yogī who is free from imperfections and is ever united with his Self, experiences easily the supreme bliss of identity with Brahman’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 109

11.109

उत्सेक उदधेर्यद्वत्कुशाग्रेणैकबिन्दुना। मनसो निग्रहस्तद्वद्भवेदपरिखेदतः॥

‘The control of the mind can be achieved by untiring practice over a long period, even as the ocean can be dried up by baling its waters out drop by drop with a blade of grass.’

Chapter 11 · Verse 110

11.110

बृहद्रथस्य राजर्षेः शाकायन्यो मुनिः सुखम्। प्राह मैत्राख्यशाखायां समाध्युक्तिपुरःसरम्॥

In the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad of the Yajur Veda, sage Sākāyanya spoke of the great bliss experienced in Samādhi to the royal sage Bṛhad-ratha while discoursing on Samādhi.

Chapter 11 · Verse 111

11.111

यथा निरिन्धनो वह्निः स्वयोनावुपशाम्यति। तथा वृत्तिक्षयाच्चित्तं स्वयोनावुपशाम्यति॥

‘As fire without fuel dies down and becomes latent in its cause, so the mind, when its modifications have been silenced, merges in its cause’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 112

11.112

स्वयोनावुपशान्तस्य मनसः सत्यकामिनः। इन्द्रियार्थविमूढस्यानृताः कर्मवशानुगाः॥

‘To the mind fixed on Reality, merged in its cause and impervious to the sensations arising from the sense-objects, the joys and sorrows (together with their occasions and materials) experienced as a result of the fructifying Karma seem unreal’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 113

11.113

चित्तमेव हि संसारस्तत्प्रयत्नेन शोधयेत्। यच्चित्तस्तन्मयो मर्त्यो गुह्यमेतत्सनातनम्॥

‘The mind is indeed the world. It should be purified with great effort. It is an ancient truth that the mind assumes the forms of the objects to which it is applied.’

Chapter 11 · Verse 114

11.114

चित्तस्य हि प्रसादेन हन्ति कर्म शुभाशुभम्। प्रसन्नात्मात्मनि स्थित्वा सुखमक्षयमश्नुते॥

‘Through the purification of his mind a man destroys the impressions of his good and evil Karma and the purified mind abiding in Ātman enjoys undiminishing bliss’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 115

11.115

समासक्तं यथा चित्तं जन्तोर्विषयगोचरे। यद्येवं ब्रह्मणि स्यात्तत्को न मुच्येत बन्धनात्॥

‘If a man were to focus his mind on Brahman, as he commonly does on the objects of senses, what bondage would he not be free from?’

Chapter 11 · Verse 116

11.116

मनो हि द्विविधं प्रोक्तं शुद्धं चाशुद्धमेव च। अशुद्धं कामसम्पर्काच्छुद्धं कामविवर्जितम्॥

‘Mind has been described as of two types, pure (śuddha) and impure (aśuddha). The impure is that which is tainted by desires, the pure is that which is free from desires’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 117

11.117

मन एव मनुष्याणां कारणं बन्धमोक्षयोः। बन्धाय विषयासक्तं मुक्त्यै निर्विषयं स्मृतम्॥

‘The mind alone is the cause of bondage and release. Attachment to objects leads to bondage and freedom from attachment to them leads to release’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 118

11.118

न शक्यते वर्णयितुं गिरा तदा स्वयं तदन्तःकरणेन गृह्यते॥

‘The bliss arising from absorption in the contemplation of the Self, when all sins and taints are washed off through the practice of Samādhi, cannot be described in words. One must feel it in one’s own heart’.

Chapter 11 · Verse 119

11.119

यद्यप्यसौ चिरं कालं समाधिर्दुर्लभो नृणाम्। तथापि क्षणिको ब्रह्मानन्दं निश्चाययत्यसौ॥

Though it is rare for men to keep their minds long in the state of absorption, still even a glimpse of it confers conviction about the bliss of Brahman.

Chapter 11 · Verse 120

11.120

श्रद्धालुर्व्यसनी योऽत्र निश्चिनोत्येव सर्वथा। निश्चिते तु सकृत्तस्मिन्विश्वसित्यन्यदाप्ययम्॥

A man who has full faith in the truth of this bliss and is ceaselessly industrious about getting it, is sure to have it even for a short while; but this is enough to convince him of its reality at other times also.

Chapter 11 · Verse 121

11.121

तादृक्पुमानुदासीनकालेऽप्यानन्दवासनाम्। उपेक्ष्य मुख्यमानन्दं भावयत्येव तत्परः॥

Such a man ignores the bliss experienced in the state of mental quiescence and is ever devoted to the supreme bliss and meditates on it.

Chapter 11 · Verse 122

11.122

परव्यसनिनी नारी व्यग्रापि गृहकर्मणि। तदेवास्वादयत्यन्तः परसङ्गरसायनम्॥

A woman devoted to a paramour, though engaged in household duties, with all the time be dwelling in mind on the pleasures with him.

Chapter 11 · Verse 123

11.123

एवं तत्त्वे परे शुद्धे धीरो विश्रान्तिमागतः। तदेवास्वादयत्यन्तर्बहिर्व्यवहारन्नपि॥

Similarly the wise one who has found peace in the supreme Reality will be ever enjoying within the bliss of Brahman even when engaged in worldly matters.

Chapter 11 · Verse 124

11.124

धीरत्वमक्षप्राबल्येऽप्यानन्दास्वादवाञ्छया। तिरस्कृत्याखिलाक्षाणि तच्चिन्तायां प्रवर्तनम्॥

Wisdom consists in subjugating the desires for sense-pleasure, even when the passions are strong and in engaging the mind in meditation on Brahman with the desire to enjoy the bliss.

Chapter 11 · Verse 125

11.125

भारवाही शिरोभारं मुक्त्वास्ते विश्रमं गतः। संसारव्यापृतित्यागे तादृग्बुद्धिस्तु विश्रमः॥

A man carrying a burden on his head feels relief when he removes the load; similarly a man freed from worldly entanglements feels he is in rest.

Chapter 11 · Verse 126

11.126

विश्रान्तिं परमां प्राप्तस्त्वौदासीन्ये यथा तथा। सुखदुःखदशायां च तदानन्दैकतत्परः॥

Thus relieved of burden and enjoying rest, he fixes his mind on the contemplation of the bliss of Brahman, whether in the state of detachment or experiencing pain or pleasure according to fructifying Karma.

Chapter 11 · Verse 127

11.127

अग्निप्रवेशहेतौ धीः शृङ्गारे यादृशी तथा। धीरस्योदेति विषयेऽनुसन्धानविरोधिनी॥

As a Satī about to enter the fire considers the delay in putting on clothes and ornaments to be irritating, so also one devoted to the achievement of the bliss of Brahman, feels about worldly objects that obstruct the practice of meditation on bliss.

Chapter 11 · Verse 128

11.128

अविरोधिसुखे बुद्धिः स्वानन्दे च गमागमौ। कुर्वन्त्यास्ते क्रमादेषा काकाक्षिवदितस्ततः॥

The sage, looking now at the bliss of Brahman and now at such worldly objects as are not opposed to it, is like a crow that turns its eye from one side to another.

Chapter 11 · Verse 129

11.129

एकैव दृष्टिः काकस्य वामदक्षिणनेत्रयोः। यात्यायात्येवमानन्दद्वये तत्त्वविदो मतिः॥

The crow has only a single vision which alternates between the right and left eye. Similarly the vision of the knower of Truth alternates between the two types of bliss (of Brahman and the world).

Chapter 11 · Verse 130

11.130

भुञ्जानो विषयानन्दं ब्रह्मानन्दं च तत्त्ववित्। द्विभाषाभिज्ञवद्विद्यादुभौ लौकिकवैदिकौ॥

Enjoying both the bliss of Brahman taught in the scriptures and the worldly bliss unopposed to it, the knower of truth knows them both in the same way as one who knows two languages.

Chapter 11 · Verse 131

11.131

दुःखप्राप्तौ न चोद्वेगो यथा पूर्वं यतो द्विदृक्। गङ्गामग्नार्धकायस्य पुंसः शीतोष्णधीर्यथा॥

When the knower experiences sufferings, he is not disturbed by them as he would have been before. Just as a man half-immersed in the cool water of the Ganges feels both the heat of the sun and the coolness of the water, so he feels the misery of the world and the bliss of Brahman at the same time.

Chapter 11 · Verse 132

11.132

इत्थं जागरणे तत्त्वविदो ब्रह्मसुखं सदा। भाति तद्वासनाजन्ये स्वप्ने तद्भासते तथा॥

The knower of truth, experiencing the bliss of Brahman in the waking state experiences it also in the dreaming state, because it is the impressions received in the waking state that give rise to dreams.

Chapter 11 · Verse 133

11.133

अविद्यावासनाप्यस्तीत्यतस्तद्वासनोत्थिते। स्वप्ने पूर्ववदेवैष सुखं दुःखं च वीक्षते॥

The impressions of ignorance still continue in the dreaming state. So in a dream a wise man will experience sometimes joy and sometimes suffering, without being affected by either.

Chapter 11 · Verse 134

11.134

ब्रह्मानन्दाभिधे ग्रन्थे ब्रह्मानन्दप्रकाशकम्। योगिप्रत्यक्षमध्याये प्रथमेऽस्मिन्नुदीरितम्॥

In this Chapter, the first of the five dealing with the bliss of Brahman, is described direct realisation of the Yogī revealing the bliss of Brahman.

Chapter 12

Chapter 12 · Verse 1

12.1

नन्वेवं वासनानन्दाद्ब्रह्मानन्दादपीतरम्। वेत्तु योगी निजानन्दं मूढस्यात्रास्ति का गतिः॥

(Question): A Yogī can enjoy the natural bliss of the Self which is different from the bliss of mental quiescence and the bliss of deep sleep; but what will happen to the ignorant man?

Chapter 12 · Verse 2

12.2

धर्माधर्मवशादेष जायतां म्रियतामपि। पुनः पुनर्देहलक्षैः किं नो दाक्षिण्यतो वद॥

(Reply): The ignorant are born in innumerable bodies and they die again and again – all owing to their righteous or unrighteous deeds. What is the use of our sympathy for them?

Chapter 12 · Verse 3

12.3

अस्ति वोऽनुजिघृक्षुवाद्दाक्षिण्येन प्रयोजनम्। तर्हि ब्रूहि स मूढः किं जिज्ञासुर्वा पराङ्मुखः॥

(Doubt): Because of the desire of the teacher to help his ignorant pupils he can do something for them. (Reply): Then you must tell whether they are willing to learn the spiritual truth or are averse to it.

Chapter 12 · Verse 4

12.4

उपास्तिं कर्म वा ब्रूयाद्विमुखाय यथोचितम्। मन्दप्रज्ञं तु जिज्ञासुमात्मानन्देन बोधयेत्॥

If they are still devoted to external objects, some suitable kind of worship or ritual can be prescribed for them. If, on the other hand, they, though spiritually dull, desire to learn the truth, they can be instructed in the knowledge of the bliss of the Self.

Chapter 12 · Verse 5

12.5

बोधयामास मैत्रेयीं याज्ञवल्क्यो निजप्रियाम्। न वा अरे पत्युरर्थे पतिः प्रिय इतीरयन्॥

Yājñavalkya instructed this by pointing out to his beloved wife, Maitreyī, that ‘a wife does not love her husband for his sake’.

Chapter 12 · Verse 6

12.6

पतिर्जाया पुत्रवित्ते पशुब्राह्मणबाहुजाः। लोका देवा वेदभूते सर्वं चात्मार्थतः प्रियम्॥

The husband, wife or son, riches or animals, Brahmanahood or Kshatriyahood, the different worlds, the gods, the Vedas, the elements and all other objects are dear to one for the sake of one’s own Self.

Chapter 12 · Verse 7

12.7

पत्याविच्छा यदा पत्न्यास्तदा प्रीतिं करोति सा। क्षुदनुष्ठानरोगाद्यैस्तदा नेच्छति तत्पतिः॥

A wife shows affection to her husband when she desires his company; the husband too reciprocates but not when he is engaged in worship or afflicted with illness, hunger and so forth.

Chapter 12 · Verse 8

12.8

पतिश्चात्मन एवार्थे न जायार्थे कदाचन। अन्योऽन्यप्रेरणेऽप्येवं स्वेच्छयैव प्रवर्तनम्॥

Her love is not for her husband’s sake but for her own. Similarly the husband’s love also is for his own satisfaction and not for hers. Thus even in the mutual love between husband and wife the incentive is one’s own desire for happiness.

Chapter 12 · Verse 9

12.9

श्मश्रुकण्टकवेधेन बालो रुदति तत्पिता। चुम्बत्येव न सा प्रीतिर्बालार्थे स्वार्थ एव सा॥

A child, when kissed by its father, may cry, being pricked by the latter’s bristly beard, still its father goes on kissing the child – it is not for its sake but for his own.

Chapter 12 · Verse 10

12.10

निरिच्छमपि रत्नादि वित्तं यत्नेन पालयन्। प्रीतिं करोति सा स्वार्थे वित्तार्थत्वं न शङ्कितम्॥

Wealth and gems have no likes or dislikes of their own, but their owner looks after them with love and care. It is for his own sake, none doubts it to be for theirs.

Chapter 12 · Verse 11

12.11

अनिच्छति बलीवर्दे विवाहयिषते बलात्। प्रीतिः सा वणिगर्थैव बलीवर्दार्थता कुतः॥

A merchant forces his bullock, though unwilling, to carry a load. He loves the bullock for his own sake, how can it be for the bullock’s?

Chapter 12 · Verse 12

12.12

ब्राह्मण्यं मेऽस्ति पूज्योऽहमिति तुष्यति पूजया। अचेतनाया जातेर्नो सन्तुष्टिः पुंस एव सा॥

A Brāhmaṇa knowing that he deserves respect, is satisfied when he receives it. This satisfaction is not felt for his caste, an insentient abstraction, but for the man himself.

Chapter 12 · Verse 13

12.13

क्षत्रियोऽहं तेन राज्यं करोमीत्यत्र राजता। न जातेर्वैश्यजात्यादौ योजनायेदमीरितम्॥

A king feels exalted that he is a Kṣatriya and hence is a ruler, but the feeling is not for the caste. The same applies to men of Vaiśya and other castes also.

Chapter 12 · Verse 14

12.14

स्वर्गलोकब्रह्मलोकौ स्तां ममेत्यभिवाञ्छनम्। लोकयोर्नोपकाराय स्वभोगायैव केवलम्॥

The desire, ‘May I attain the region of heaven or of Brahmā’, is not for the well-being of those regions but only for one’s own enjoyment.

Chapter 12 · Verse 15

12.15

ईशविष्ण्वादयो देवाः पूज्यन्ते पापनष्टये। न तन्निष्पापदेवार्थं स्वार्थं तत्तूपयुज्यते॥

People worship Śiva, Viṣṇu and other deities to destroy sins. It is not for the sake of the deities who are already free from sins, but for their own sake.

Chapter 12 · Verse 16

12.16

ऋगादयो ह्यधीयन्ते दुर्ब्राह्मण्यानवाप्तये। न तत् प्रसक्तं वेदेषु मनुष्येषु प्रसज्यते॥

The Brāhmaṇas study the Ṛg and other Vedas to avoid falling from their (respectable) Brahminhood; this applies to men only and not to the Vedas.

Chapter 12 · Verse 17

12.17

भूम्यादिपञ्चभूतानि स्थानतृट्पाकशोषणैः। हेतुभिश्चावकाशेन वाञ्छन्त्येषां न हेतवे॥

People want the five elements, viz., earth, water, fire, air and Ākāśa, because of their usefulness to them in giving shelter, quenching their thirst, cooking, drying and space for movement and not for the sake of the elements themselves.

Chapter 12 · Verse 18

12.18

स्वामिभृत्यादिकं सर्वं स्वोपकाराया वाञ्छति। तत्तत्कृतोपकारस्तु तस्य तस्य न विद्यते॥

People desire to have servants or masters for their own benefit and not for the benefit of (servants or masters) themselves.

Chapter 12 · Verse 19

12.19

सर्वव्यवहृतिष्वेवमनुसन्धातुमीदृशम्। उदाहरणबाहुल्यं तेन स्वां वासयेन्मतिम्॥

There are plenty of such examples to enable one to study and come to the same conclusion on all occasions. By these one should convince one’s mind that for every man the Self is the only real object of love.

Chapter 12 · Verse 20

12.20

रागो वध्वादि विषये श्रद्धा यागादि कर्मणि। भक्तिः स्याद्गुरुदेवादाविच्छा त्वप्राप्तवस्तुनि॥

(Doubt): What type of love is it that the scriptures say is felt towards the Self? Is it the passionate attachment which is felt towards wife and other objects, the faith which is experienced in sacrifices and other rituals, the devotion which a man cherishes towards God and his teacher or is it the desire one feels for something one does not possess?

Chapter 12 · Verse 21

12.21

तर्ह्यस्तु सात्विकी वृत्तिः सुखमात्रानुवर्तिनी। प्राप्ते नष्टेऽपि सद्भावादिच्छतो व्यतिरिच्यते॥

(Reply): The real love of the Self is that which, in the absence of these emotions, manifests itself owing to the preponderance of Sāttvikā quality in the intellect. This love of the Self is different from desire, for it exists even when desire is present or destroyed.

Chapter 12 · Verse 22

12.22

सुखसाधनतोपाधेरन्नपानादयः प्रियाः॥

(Doubt): Be it so, but food, drink etc., are liked because of their quality of giving happiness (and not for their own sake).

Chapter 12 · Verse 23

12.23

आत्मानुकुल्यादन्नादिसमश्चेदमुनात्र कः। अनुकुलयितव्यः स्यान्नैकस्मिन्कर्मकर्तृता॥

If you say that the Self is also a means to happiness like food and drink, then we ask: who is it that enjoys happiness? One and the same thing cannot be both the subject and the object of enjoyment.

Chapter 12 · Verse 24

12.24

सुखे वैषयिके प्रीतिमात्रमात्मा त्वतिप्रियः। सुखे व्यभिचरत्येषा नात्मनि व्यभिचारिणी॥

Love for the means to happiness is partial love, but the love for the Self is infinite. The love for the means passes from one object to another, but the love for the Self is steadfast.

Chapter 12 · Verse 25

12.25

एकं त्यक्त्वान्यदादत्ते सुखं वैषयिकं सदा। नात्मा त्याज्यो न चादेयस्तस्मिन्व्यभिचरेत्कथम्॥

Love for an object of happiness always passes from one to another; (they are objects that can be accepted or rejected); but the Self cannot be treated like that; so how can love of Self change?

Chapter 12 · Verse 26

12.26

हानादानविहीनोऽस्मिन्नुपेक्षा चेत्तृणादिवत्। उपेक्षितुः स्वरूपत्वान्नोपेक्ष्यत्वं निजात्मनः॥

(Doubt): Even though it cannot be accepted or rejected the Self may be regarded as an object of indifference, like a piece of straw. (Reply): No, because it is the very Self of the person who is to regard it with indifference.

Chapter 12 · Verse 27a

12.27a

रोगक्रोधाभिभूतानां मुमूर्षा वीक्ष्यते क्वचित्। ततो द्वेषाद्भवेत्त्याज्य आत्मेति यदि तन्न हि॥

(Doubt): People begin to hate the Self when they are overpowered by disease or anger and wish to die. (Reply): This is not so.

Chapter 12 · Verse 28a

12.28a

त्यक्तुं योग्यस्य देहस्य नात्मता त्यक्तुरेव सा। न त्यक्तर्यस्ति स द्वेषस्त्याज्ये द्वेषे तु का क्षतिः॥

When they desire to do away with the body it is an object for rejection, not their Self. The Self is the subject that desires the end of the body and it feels no hatred for itself. What harm is there if they hate the body, an object?

Chapter 12 · Verse 27b

12.27b

आत्मार्थत्वेन सर्वस्य प्रीतेश्चात्मा ह्यतिप्रियः। यथा पितुः पुत्रमित्रात्पुत्रः प्रियतरस्तथा॥

All objects are desired for the sake of the Self and hence of all the objects that are loved the Self is dearest. A man’s son is dearer to him than his son’s friends.

Chapter 12 · Verse 28b

12.28b

मा न भूवमहं किन्तु भूयासं सर्वदेत्यसौ। आशीः सर्वस्य दृस्तेति प्रत्यक्षा प्रीतिरात्मनि॥

‘May I never perish, may I ever exist’ is the desire seen in all. So love for the Self is quite evident.

Chapter 12 · Verse 29

12.29

इत्यादिभिस्त्रिभिः प्रीतौ सिद्धायामेवमात्मनि। पुत्रभार्यादिशेषत्वमात्मनः कैश्चिदिर्रितम्॥

Though the Self as the object of the highest love is taught by the scriptures and proved both by reasoning and experience, there are some who hold that the Self is merely secondary to son, wife etc., as an object of love.

Chapter 12 · Verse 30

12.30

एतद्विवक्षया पुत्रे मुख्यात्मत्वं श्रुतीरितम्। आत्मा वै पुत्रनामेति तच्चोपनिषदि स्फुटम्॥

To support this they quote the Śruti: ‘The son indeed is the Self’, which shows the superiority of the son. This has been clearly spoken of in the Upaniṣad.

Chapter 12 · Verse 31

12.31

सोऽस्यायमात्मा पुण्येभ्यः कर्मेभ्यः प्रतिधीयते। अथास्येतर आत्मायं कृतकृत्यः प्रमीयते॥

‘The (father’s) Self, born in the form of the son, becomes his substitute for the performance of meritorious deeds. The Self of the father, having fulfilled its purpose (by begetting a son) and having reached old age, departs’.

Chapter 12 · Verse 32

12.32

सत्यप्यात्मनि लोकोऽस्ति नापुत्रस्यात एव हि। अनुशिष्टं पुत्रमेव लोक्यमाहुर्मनीषिणः॥

A verse in the Bṛhad-āraṇyaka Upaniṣad says that in spite of the existence of the Self a man who has no son does not go to heaven. So the thinkers said that a son who is well trained in the Vedas helps his father to attain heaven.

Chapter 12 · Verse 33

12.33

मनुष्यलोको जय्यः स्यात्पुत्रेणैवेतरेण नो। मुमूर्षुर्मन्त्रयेत्पुत्रं त्वं ब्रह्मेत्यादिमन्त्रकैः॥

The joys of this world can be attained through the son and not by other things. The dying father therefore should instruct his son the Vedic truth, ‘You are Brahman’.

Chapter 12 · Verse 34

12.34

इत्यादिश्रुतयः प्राहुः पुत्रभार्यादिशेषताम्। लौकिका अपि पुत्रस्य प्राधान्यमनुमन्यते॥

These Vedic verses are quoted to prove the importance of son, wife and so forth (and one’s own Self as secondary). Ordinary people too admit the greater importance of a son.

Chapter 12 · Verse 35

12.35

स्वस्मिन्मृतेऽपि पुत्रादिर्जीवेद्वित्तादिना यथा। तथैव यत्नं कुरुते मुख्याः पुत्रादयस्ततः॥

A father labours hard to acquire wealth for the maintenance of his sons and others after his death. Hence the son is superior to the Self.

Chapter 12 · Verse 36

12.36

बाधमेतावता नात्मा शेषो भवति कस्य चित्। गौणमिथ्यामुख्यभेदैरात्मायं भवति त्रिधा॥

All right, but these texts do not prove the Self to be less important. It is to be remembered that the word ‘Self’ is used in three senses, figurative (gauṇa), illusory (mithyā) and fundamental (mukhya).

Chapter 12 · Verse 37

12.37

देवदत्तस्तु सिंहोऽयमित्यैक्यं गौणमेतयोः। भेदस्य भासमानत्वात्पुत्रादेरात्मता तथा॥

In the expression ‘Deva-datta is a lion’, the identification is figurative, for the difference between the two is evident. Similar is the case of the son and others as the Self.

Chapter 12 · Verse 38

12.38

भेदोऽस्ति पञ्चकोषेषु साक्षिणो न तु भात्यसौ। मिथ्यात्मतातः कोषाणां स्थाणोर्चौरात्मता यथा॥

Difference exists between the five sheaths and the Witness, though it is not evident and so the sheaths are illusory, like the thief seen in the stump of a tree.

Chapter 12 · Verse 39

12.39

न भाति भेदो नाप्यस्ति साक्षिणोऽप्रतियोगिनः। सर्वान्तरत्वात् तस्यैव मुख्यमात्मत्वमिष्यते॥

The witness-consciousness is without a second and therefore in it there neither appears nor is any difference. As it is the innermost essence it is accepted that the word ‘Self’ in its fundamental sense refers to the Witness itself.

Chapter 12 · Verse 40

12.40

सत्येवं व्यवहारेषु येषु यस्यात्मतोचिता। तेषु तस्यैव शेषित्वं सर्वस्यान्यस्य शेषता॥

As the word ‘Self’ has these three meanings in daily use the suitable one becomes primary, the other two becoming merely secondary.

Chapter 12 · Verse 41

12.41

मुमूर्षोर्गृहरक्षादौ गौणात्मैवोपयुज्यते। न मुख्यात्मा न मिथ्यात्मा पुत्रः शेषी भवत्यतः॥

In the case of a dying man, giving charge of the family property and tradition to his son, the figurative meaning of ‘Self’ fits in, not the primary or the illusory meaning.

Chapter 12 · Verse 42

12.42

अध्येता वह्निरित्यत्र सन्नप्यग्निर्न गृह्यते। अयोग्यत्वेन योग्यत्वाद्बटुरेवात्र गृह्यते॥

In the sentence ‘the reciter is the fire’ the term ‘reciter’ cannot actually refer to fire, for the latter is incapable of reciting, but must mean a Brahma-cāri who is able to do so.

Chapter 12 · Verse 43

12.43

कृशोऽहं पुष्टिमाप्स्यामीत्यादौ देहात्मतोचिता। न पुत्रं विनियुङ्क्तेऽत्र पुष्टिहेत्वन्नभक्षणे॥

In such expressions as ‘I am thin and I must get fatter’, the body should be taken as the Self. For the sake of one’s own growing fat nobody engages his son in eating.

Chapter 12 · Verse 44

12.44

तपसा स्वर्गमेष्यामीत्यादौ कर्त्रात्मतोचिता। अनपेक्ष्य वपुर्भोगं चरेत्कृच्छ्रादिकं ततः॥

In such expressions as ‘I shall attain heaven by austerities’ the doer (the intellect-sheath) should be regarded as the Self. So ignoring the physical enjoyment people practise severe austerities.

Chapter 12 · Verse 45

12.45

मोक्ष्येऽहमित्यत्र युक्तं चिदात्मत्वं तदा पुमान्। तद्वेत्ति गुरुशास्त्राभ्यां न तु किंचिच्चिकीर्षति॥

When a man says, ‘I shall be free’, he then acquires knowledge (of the Self) from the teacher and the scripture and desires nothing else. Here the word ‘I’ should be regarded as the witness Self.

Chapter 12 · Verse 46

12.46

विप्रक्षत्रादयो यद्वद्बृहस्पतिसवादिषु। व्यवस्थितास्तथा गौणमिथ्यामुख्या यथोचितम्॥

Just as Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are entitled to perform the sacrifices called Bṛhaspati-sava, Rāja-sūya and Vaiśya-stoma according to their fitness, so the figurative, illusory and fundamental selves are meant in different contexts.

Chapter 12 · Verse 47

12.47

तत्र तत्रोचिते प्रीतिरात्मन्येवातिशायिनी। अनात्मनि तु तच्छेषे प्रीतिरन्यत्र नोभयम्॥

Infinite love is always left for the Self which is primary in any particular context; and for whatever is related to it there is just moderate love and for all other things there is no love whatsoever.

Chapter 12 · Verse 48

12.48

उपेक्ष्यं द्वेष्यमित्यन्यत् द्वेधा मार्गतृणादिकम्। उपेक्ष्यं व्याघ्रसर्पादि द्वेष्यमेवं चतुर्विधम्॥

Other things are of two kinds, to be ignored or hated. Straws lying on the road are disregarded, whereas tigers and snakes are hated. So things are of four kinds: loved, dearly loved, disregarded or hated.

Chapter 12 · Verse 49

12.49

आत्मा शेष उपेक्ष्यं च द्वेष्यं चेति चतुर्ष्वपि। न व्यक्तिनियमः किन्तु तत्तत्कार्यात्तथा तथा॥

The Self, things related to the Self and objects to be disregarded or hated – of these four categories of things there is no sacro-sanctity attached to any one of them that it would always be primary or secondary etc. But it (their being primary or secondary etc.,) depends on the effect they produce under particular circumstances.

Chapter 12 · Verse 50

12.50

स्याद्व्याघ्रः संमुखो द्वेष्यो ह्युपेक्ष्यस्तु पराङ्मुखः। लालनादनुकूलश्चेद्विनोदायेति शेषताम्॥

When a tiger confronts man, it is hated; when it is away, it is disregarded; and when it has been tamed and made friendly, it causes joy; thus it is related to him and is loved.

Chapter 12 · Verse 51

12.51

व्यक्तीनां नियमो मा भूल्लक्षणात्तुव्यवस्थितिः। आनुकूल्यं प्रातिकूल्यं द्वयाभावश्च लक्षणम्॥

Even though no thing is primary or secondary by itself, there are some characteristics to distinguish them under certain circumstances. These characteristics are: their being favourable, unfavourable, or neither of these.

Chapter 12 · Verse 52

12.52

आत्मा प्रेयान्प्रियः शेषो द्वेष्योपेक्ष्ये तदन्ययोः। इति व्यवस्थितो लोको याज्ञवल्क्यमतं च तत्॥

The popular conclusion is that the Self is the dearest, the objects related to it are dear and the rest are either disregarded or hated. This is also the verdict of Yājñavalkya.

Chapter 12 · Verse 53

12.53

अन्यत्रापि श्रुतिः प्राह पुत्राद्वित्तात्तथान्यतः। सर्वस्मादान्तरं तत्त्वं तदेतत्प्रेय ईक्षताम्॥

Elsewhere too the Śruti declares: ‘Know this Self as the dearest which is more intrinsic than son, wealth and so forth’.

Chapter 12 · Verse 54

12.54

श्रौत्या विचारदृष्ट्यायं साक्ष्येवात्मा न चेतरः। कोषान्पञ्च विविच्यान्तर्वस्तुदृष्टिर्विचारणा॥

Through the eye of discrimination following the Śruti it becomes clear that the witness-consciousness is the real Self. Discrimination means separating the five sheaths and seeing the inner substance.

Chapter 12 · Verse 55

12.55

जागरस्वप्नसुप्तीनामागमापायभासनम्। यतो भवत्यसावात्मा स्वप्रकाशचिदात्मकः॥

That is the self-luminous consciousness, the Self, which is the witness of the presence and absence of the states of waking, dreaming and deep sleep.

Chapter 12 · Verse 56

12.56

शेषाः प्राणादिवित्तान्ता आसन्नास्तारतम्यतः। प्रीतिस्तथा तारतम्यात्तेषु सर्वेषु वीक्ष्यते॥

The various objects of enjoyment, from life down to wealth, are objects of varying degrees of love according to their proximity to the Self.

Chapter 12 · Verse 57

12.57

वित्तात्पुत्रः प्रियः पुत्रात्पिण्डः पिण्डात्तथेन्द्रियम्। इन्द्रियाच्च प्रियः प्राणः प्राणादात्मा परः प्रियः॥

A son is dearer than wealth, the body dearer than the son, the sense-organs dearer than the body, life and mind dearer than the sense organs and the Self is supremely dearer than life and mind.

Chapter 12 · Verse 58

12.58

एवं स्थिते विवादोऽत्र प्रतिबुद्धविमूढयोः। श्रुत्योदाहारि तत्रात्मा प्रेयानित्येव निर्णयः॥

In the Śruti there is a dialogue between a wise and a dull-witted man which illustrates the point that the Self is the dearest of all objects.

Chapter 12 · Verse 59

12.59

साक्ष्येव दृश्यादन्यस्मात्प्रेयानित्याह तत्त्ववित्। प्रेयान्पुत्रादिरेवेमं भोक्तुं साक्षीति मूढधीः॥

The wise man holds that the witness-consciousness, is dearer than all objects. The dull-witted man maintains that son and other objects are dearer and that the witness-consciousness enjoys the happiness caused by these objects.

Chapter 12 · Verse 60

12.60

आत्मनोऽन्यं प्रियं ब्रूते शिष्यश्च प्रतिवाद्यपि। तस्योत्तरं वाचो बोधशापौ कुर्यात्तयोः क्रमात्॥

The ignorant disciple and the confirmed opponent both assert that something other than the Self (Ātman) is the object of greatest love. The reply given will prove to be an instruction to the disciple and a curse to the confirmed opponent.

Chapter 12 · Verse 61

12.61

प्रियं त्वां रोत्स्यतीत्येवमुत्तरं वक्ति तत्त्ववित्। स्वोक्तप्रियस्य दुष्टत्वं शिष्यो वेत्ति विवेकतः॥

The wise man quotes the scripture in his reply: ‘Your dearest thing will make you weep’. The pupil analyses this reply and finds out his error in considering something other than the Self as the dearest.

Chapter 12 · Verse 62

12.62

अलभ्यमानस्तनयः पितरौ क्लेशयेच्चिरम्। लब्धोऽपि गर्भपातेन प्रसवेन च बाधते॥

When a married couple desire to have a son and do not have one, they are disappointed and miserable. After conception, a miscarriage or the pain of labour causes sorrow.

Chapter 12 · Verse 63

12.63

जातस्य ग्रहरोगादि कुमारस्य च मूकता। उपनीतेऽप्यविद्यत्वमनुद्वाहश्च पण्डिते॥

When a son is born he may suffer from diseases or from the position of the planets at his birth, or he may be stupid or obstinate, or after the investiture of sacred thread, he may study nothing or if he is learned, he may remain unmarried.

Chapter 12 · Verse 64

12.64

पुनश्च परदारादि दारिद्र्यं च कुटुम्बिनः। पित्रोः दुःखस्य नास्त्यन्तो धनी चेन्म्रियते तदा॥

Again he may start pursuing the wives of others, or he may have an unwieldy family and remain in poverty, or he may grow wealthy and yet die in his youth. Infinite are the sorrows of parents.

Chapter 12 · Verse 65

12.65

एवं विविच्य पुत्रादौ प्रीतिं त्यक्त्वा निजात्मनि। निश्चित्य परमां प्रीतिं वीक्षते तमहर्निशम्॥

Having considered all this, the disciple must abstain from forming an attachment to other things. He should focus his love on the Self and contemplate It day and night.

Chapter 12 · Verse 66

12.66

आग्रहाद्ब्रह्मविद्द्वेषादपि पक्षममुञ्चतः। वादिनो नरकः प्रोक्तो दोषश्च बहुयोनिषु॥

The confirmed opponent, who does not give up his contention due to obstinacy and hostility to the knower of truth, sinks into the depths of darkness and suffers the pains of innumerable births.

Chapter 12 · Verse 67

12.67

ब्रह्मविद्ब्रह्मरूपत्वादीश्वरस्तेन वर्णितम्। यद्यत्तत्तत्तथैव स्यात्तच्छिष्यप्रतिवादिनोः॥

The knower of Brahman is of the nature of Brahman and is described as Īśvara, the all-powerful. Whatever he says will come to pass for the pupil and the opponent.

Chapter 12 · Verse 68

12.68

यस्तु साक्षिणमात्मानं सेवते प्रियमुत्तमम्। तस्य प्रेयानसावात्मा न नश्यति कदाचन॥

He who contemplates the witness Self as the dearest of all objects will find that this dearest Self never suffers destruction.

Chapter 12 · Verse 69

12.69

परप्रेमास्पदत्वेन परमानन्दरूपता। सुखवृद्धिः प्रीतिवृद्धौ सार्वभौमादिषु श्रुता॥

The Supreme Self, being the object of dearest love, is the source of infinite joy. The Śruti has it that from the sovereignty of this world to position of Hiraṇya-garbha, everywhere, wherever there is greater love there is greater bliss.

Chapter 12 · Verse 70

12.70

चैतन्यवत्सुखं चास्य स्वभावश्चेच्चिदात्मनः। धीवृत्तिष्वनुवर्तेत सर्वास्वपि चितिर्यथा॥

(Doubt): If the nature of the Self is bliss as well as consciousness, bliss should be found in all the modifications of the mind, as is consciousness.

Chapter 12 · Verse 71

12.71

मैवमुष्णप्रकाशात्मा दीपस्तस्य प्रभा गृहे। व्याप्नोति नोष्णता तद्वच्चितेरेवानुवर्तनम्॥

(Reply): Not so. A lamp burning in a room emits both light and heat, but it is only the light that fills the room and not heat; similarly, it is only consciousness which accomplishes the Vṛttis (and not bliss).

Chapter 12 · Verse 72

12.72

गन्धरूपरसस्पर्शेष्वपि सत्सु यथा पृथक्। एकाक्षेणैक एवार्थो गृह्यते नेतरस्तथा॥

An object may be characterised by odour, colour, taste and touch, yet each of these properties is cognised by one particular sense-organ and not the others. It is the same with the bliss of the Self.

Chapter 12 · Verse 73

12.73

चिदानन्दौ नैव भिन्नौ गन्धाद्यास्तु विलक्षणाः। इति चेत् तदभेदोऽपि साक्षिण्यन्यत्र वा वद॥

(Doubt): Odours, taste and so forth differ from one another, but in the Self consciousness and bliss are identical. (Reply): Tell whether this identity is in the witness Self or elsewhere?

Chapter 12 · Verse 74

12.74

आद्ये गन्धादयोऽप्येवमभिन्नाः पुष्पवर्तिनः। अक्षभेदेन तद्भेदे वृत्तिभेदात्तयोर्भिदा॥

The odour, colour and other properties of a flower are not separate from one another in the flower. If it be said that the separation of these properties is brought about by the sense-organs, we rejoin that the seeming difference between consciousness and bliss is produced by (the predominance of Rajas or Sattva in) the Vṛttis.

Chapter 12 · Verse 75

12.75

सत्ववृत्तौ चित्सुखैक्यं तद्वृत्तेर्निर्मलत्वतः। रजोवृत्तेस्तु मालिन्यात्सुखांशोऽत्र तिरस्कृतः॥

When there is a predominance of Sattva in the Vṛttis, we realise, because of their purity, that bliss and consciousness are one and the same, but when Rajas predominates, because of its impurity, the bliss is obscured.

Chapter 12 · Verse 76

12.76

तिन्तिणीफलमत्यम्लं लवणेन युतं यदा। तदाम्लस्य तिरस्कारादीषदग्नं यथा तथा॥

As the intensely sour taste of tamarind when mixed with salt is lessened and taste less sour, so with bliss (when it is obscured by Rajas).

Chapter 12 · Verse 77

12.77

ननु प्रियतमत्वेन परमानन्दतात्मनि। विवेक्तुं शक्यतामेवं विना योगेन किं भवेत्॥

(Doubt): By discrimination one can feel that the Self is the dearest, but without the practice of Yoga what good is it (for liberation)?

Chapter 12 · Verse 78

12.78

यद्योगेन तदेवैति वदामो ज्ञानसिद्धये। योगः प्रोक्तो विवेकेन ज्ञानं किं नोपजायते॥

(Reply): The goal which is reached by Yoga can also be reached by discrimination. Yoga is a means to knowledge; doesn’t knowledge arise from discrimination?

Chapter 12 · Verse 79

12.79

यत् साङ्ख्यैः प्राप्यते स्थानं तद्योगैरपि गम्यते। इति स्मृतं फलैकत्वं योगिनां च विवेकिनाम्॥

‘The state achieved by the Sāṅkhyas is also achieved by the Yogīs’. Thus it has been said in the Gītā about the identity of the fruit of both Yoga and discrimination (viveka).

Chapter 12 · Verse 80

12.80

असाध्यः कस्यचिद्योगः कस्यचिज्ज्ञाननिश्चयः। इत्थं विचार्यमार्गौ द्वौ जगाद परमेश्वरः॥

Knowing that for some Yoga is difficult and for some others knowledge, the great Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa speaks of these two paths.

Chapter 12 · Verse 81

12.81

योगे कोऽतिशयस्तेऽत्र ज्ञानमुक्तं समं द्वयोः। रागद्वेषाद्यभावश्च तुल्यो योगिविवेकिनोः॥

What speciality is there in Yoga when knowledge has been declared as common to both? Both the Yogī and the Vivekī (he who practises discrimination) are alike freed from attachment and aversion.

Chapter 12 · Verse 82

12.82

न प्रीतिर्विषयेष्वस्ति प्रेयानात्मेति जानतः। कुतो रागः कुतो द्वेषः प्रातिकूल्यमपश्यतः॥

One who knows the Self as the dearest has no love for any object of enjoyment. So how can he have attachment? And how can he who sees no object inimical to himself have any aversion?

Chapter 12 · Verse 83

12.83

देहादेः प्रतिकूलेषु द्वेषस्तुल्योद्वयोरपि। द्वेषं कुर्वन्न योगी चेदविवेक्यपि तादृशः॥

Both the Yogī and the Vivekī dislike objects unfavourable to the body, mind etc. If it be said that he who has aversion for such objects is not a Yogī, then we rejoin that equally so is he not a Vivekī.

Chapter 12 · Verse 84

12.84

द्वैतस्य प्रतिभानं तु व्यवहारे द्वयोः समम्। समाधौ नेति चेत्तद्वन्नाद्वैतत्वविवेकिनः॥

It may be said that though in the world of relative experience both accept the conception of duality, the Yogī has the advantage that there is no duality for him while in the state of Samādhi. Our reply is that he who practises discrimination about the non-duality does not experience duality at that time.

Chapter 12 · Verse 85

12.85

विवक्ष्यते तदस्माभिरद्वैतानन्दनामके। अध्याये हि तृतीये तत्सर्वमप्यतिमङ्गलम्॥

In the next chapter, called the ‘Bliss of Non-duality’ we will enlarge on the theme of the absence of duality. Therefore things told till now are free from defects.

Chapter 12 · Verse 86

12.86

सदा पश्यन्निजानन्दमपश्यन्नखिलं जगत्। अर्थाद्योगीति चेत्तर्हि सन्तुष्टो वर्धतां भवान्॥

(Doubt): He is a true Yogī who in his contemplation is ever-conscious of the bliss of the Self and is unconscious of the external world. (Reply): May the blessings of contentment ever abide with you. (For the point is gained, this is the position of the Vivekin also).

Chapter 12 · Verse 87

12.87

ब्रह्मानन्दभिधे ग्रन्थे मन्दानुग्रहसिद्धये। द्वितीयेऽध्याय एतस्मिन्नात्मानन्दो विवेचितः॥

In this second chapter of the section in which the bliss of Brahman is discussed (Chapter 11) we have dealt with the bliss of the Self (Ātmānanda) for the good of persons of spiritually dull intellect.

Chapter 13

Chapter 13 · Verse 1

13.1

योगानन्दः पुरोक्तो यः स आत्मानन्द इष्यताम्। कथं ब्रह्मत्वमेतस्य सद्वयस्येति चेच्छृणु॥

The bliss of Yoga which was described earlier may be said to be the bliss of the Self. (Doubt): How can the bliss of the embodied Self which is in duality be identical with the bliss of Brahman (who is non-dual)? (Reply): Please listen.

Chapter 13 · Verse 2

13.2

आकाशादि स्वदेहान्तं तैत्तिरीयश्रुतीरितम्। जगन्नास्त्यन्यदानन्दादद्वैतब्रह्मता ततः॥

As described in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, the whole world, from Ākāśa to the physical body, is not different from bliss. Therefore the bliss of the Self is of the nature of the non-dual Brahman.

Chapter 13 · Verse 3

13.3

आनन्दाद्ध्येव तज्जातं तिष्ठत्यानन्द एव तत्। आनन्द एव लीनं चेत्युक्तानन्दात्कथं पृथक्॥

The world is born of bliss, it abides in bliss and is merged in bliss. How then can it be anything other than this bliss?

Chapter 13 · Verse 4

13.4

कुलालाद्घट उत्पन्नो भिन्नश्चेति न शङ्क्यताम्। मृद्वदेषः उपादानं न निमित्तं कुलालवत्॥

The pot made by a potter is different from him, but let this not create any doubt, for like the clay, bliss is the material cause of the universe, not like the potter the efficient cause.

Chapter 13 · Verse 5

13.5

स्थितिर्लयश्च कुम्भस्य कुलाले स्तो न हि क्वचित्। दृष्टौ तौ मृदि तद्वत्स्यादुपादानं तयोः श्रुतेः॥

The existence and destruction of the pot are never seen to rest in the potter, but its material cause, the clay. Similarly, according to the Śruti passages their (the existence and destruction of the universe) material cause is bliss.

Chapter 13 · Verse 6

13.6

उपादानं त्रिधा भिन्नं विवर्ति परिणामि च। आरम्भकं च तत्रान्त्यौ न निरंशेऽवकाशिनौ॥

The material cause is of three kinds: (1) the Vivarta, which gives rise to a phenomenal appearance, not materially related to the cause; (2) the Pariṇāma which gives rise to an effect which is a modification or change of state of the cause; and (3) the Ārambha, which consists of effect being different from the causes. The last two (which presuppose parts) have no scope with reference to partless Brahman.

Chapter 13 · Verse 7

13.7

आरम्भवादिनोऽन्यस्मादन्यस्योत्पत्तिमूचिरे। तन्तोः पटस्य निष्पत्तेर्भिन्नौ तन्तुपटौ खलु॥

The Ārambha-vādins accept the production of one kind of material from another, as cloth from threads and they consider threads and cloth to be quite different.

Chapter 13 · Verse 8

13.8

अवस्थान्तरतापत्तिरेकस्य परिणामिता। स्यात् क्षीरं दधि मृत्कुम्भः सुवर्णं कुण्डलं यथा॥

Pariṇāma is the change of one state of the same substance into another, as milk into curd, clay into a pot and gold into an ear-ring.

Chapter 13 · Verse 9

13.9

अवस्थान्तरभानं तु विवर्तो रज्जुसर्पवत्। निरंशेऽप्यस्त्यसौ व्योम्नि तलमालिन्यकल्पनात्॥

But Vivarta is mere appearance of change of a thing or its state, not a real change: like a rope appearing as a snake. It is seen even in a partless substance, e.g., the Ākāśa (which has no shape or colour) appearing as the blue dome.

Chapter 13 · Verse 10

13.10

ततो निरंश आनन्दे विवर्तो जगदिष्यताम्। मायाशक्तिः कल्पिका स्यादैन्द्र जालिकशक्तिवत्॥

So the illusive appearance of the world in the partless bliss can be explained. Like the power of a magician, the power of Māyā may be said to bring the objective world into being.

Chapter 13 · Verse 11

13.11

शक्तिः शक्तात्पृथङ्नास्ति तद्वद्दृष्टेर्न चाभिदा। प्रतिबन्धस्य दृष्टत्वाच्छक्त्यभावे तु कस्य सः॥

Power does not exist apart from the possessor of power, for it is always seen as inseparable from him. Nor can it be said to be identical with him, for its obstruction is met with. If identical, in the absence of power, of what is the obstruction?

Chapter 13 · Verse 12

13.12

शक्तेः कार्यानुमेयत्वादकार्ये प्रतिबन्धनम्। ज्वलतोऽग्नेरदाहे स्यान्मन्त्रादि प्रतिबन्धता॥

Power is inferred from its effect. When its effects are not seen we conclude that there is some obstruction to it. For instance, if the flames of a fire do not burn, we infer the presence of some obstruction, such as incantation etc.

Chapter 13 · Verse 13

13.13

देवात्मशक्तिं स्वगुणैर्निगूढां मुनयोऽविदन्। परास्य शक्तिर्विविधा क्रियाज्ञानबलात्मिका॥

The sages perceived that the power of Brahman called Māyā is concealed by its own qualities. Many are the aspects of this divine power, which is manifest as action, knowledge and will.

Chapter 13 · Verse 14

13.14

इति वेदवचः प्राह वसिष्ठश्च तथाब्रवीत्। सर्वशक्तिपरं ब्रह्म नित्यमापूर्णमद्वयम्॥

‘The supreme Brahman is eternal, perfect, non-dual and omnipotent’, so says the Veda and Vasiṣṭha supports this.

Chapter 13 · Verse 15

13.15

यथोल्लसति शक्त्यासौ प्रकाशमधिगच्छति। चिच्छक्तिर्ब्रह्मणो राम! शरीरेषूपलभ्यते॥

‘With whatever power He means to sport, that power becomes manifest. O Rāma, the power of Brahman which manifests itself as consciousness is felt in the bodies of all beings’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 16

13.16

स्पन्दशक्तिश्च वातेषु दार्ढ्यशक्तिस्तथोपले। द्रवशक्तिस्तथाम्भःसु दाहशक्तिस्तथानले॥

‘This power abides as movement in the air, as hardness in stone, as liquidity in water, as the power to burn in fire’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 17

13.17

शून्यशक्तिस्तथाकाशे नाशशक्तिर्विनाशिनि। यथाण्डान्तर्महासर्पो जगदस्ति तथात्मनि॥

‘Similarly it abides as emptiness in Ākāśa and as perishability in the objects which are subject to destruction. As a huge serpent is latent in the egg, so the world is latent in the Self’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 18

13.18

फलपत्रलतापुष्पशाखाविटपमूलवान्। वृक्षबीजे यथा वृक्षस्तथेदं ब्रह्मणि स्थितम्॥

‘Just as a tree with its fruits, leaves, tendrils, flowers, branches, twigs and roots is latent in the seed, so does this world abide in Brahman’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 19

13.19

क्वचित्कश्चित्कदाचिच्च तस्मादुद्यन्ति शक्तयः। देशकालविचित्रत्वात्क्ष्मातलादिव शालयः॥

‘Due to variations in space and time, somewhere, some times, some powers emanate from Brahman, just as varieties of paddy from the earth.’

Chapter 13 · Verse 20

13.20

स आत्मा सर्वगो राम! नित्योदितमहावपुः। यन्मनाङ्मननीं शक्तिं धत्ते तन्मन उच्यते॥

‘O Rāma, when the all-pervasive, eternal and infinite Self assumes the power of cognition, we call it the mind.’

Chapter 13 · Verse 21

13.21

इत्यादिका स्थितिरियं हि गता प्रतिष्ठाम् आख्यायिका सुभगबालजनोदितेव॥

‘O Prince, first arises the mind, then the notion of bondage and release and then the universe consisting of many worlds. Thus all this manifestation has been fixed or settled (in human minds), like the tales told to amuse children’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 22

13.22

बालस्य हि विनोदाय धात्री शक्ति शुभां कथाम्। क्वचित्सन्ति महाबाहो! राजपुत्रास्त्रयः शुभाः॥

‘To amuse a child, O mighty one, the nurse relates some beautiful story: Once upon a time there were three handsome princes’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 23

13.23

द्वौ न जातौ तथैकस्तु गर्भ एव हि न स्थितः। वसन्ति ते धर्मयुता अत्यन्तासति पत्तने॥

‘Two of them were never born and the third was never even conceived in his mother’s womb. They lived righteously in a city which never existed.’

Chapter 13 · Verse 24

13.24

स्वकीयाच्छून्यनगरान्निर्गत्य विमलाशयाः। गच्छन्तो गगने वृक्षान्ददृशुः फलशालिनः॥

‘These holy princes came out of their city of non-existence and while roaming saw trees, laden with fruits, growing in the sky’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 25

13.25

भविष्यन्नगरे तत्र राजपुत्रास्त्रयोऽपि ते। सुखमद्य स्थिता पुत्र! मृगयाव्यवहारिणः॥

‘Then the three princes, my child, went to a city which was yet to be built and lived there happily, passing their time in games and hunting’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 26

13.26

धात्र्यैवं कथिता राम! बालकाख्यायिका शुभा। निश्चयं स ययौ बालो निर्विचारणया धिया॥

‘O Rāma, the nurse thus narrated the beautiful children’s tale. The child too through want of discrimination believed it to be true’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 27

13.27

इयं संसार रचना विचारोज्झितचेतसाम्। बालकाख्यायिकेवेत्थमवस्थितिमुपागता॥

‘Thus to those who have no discrimination the world appears to be real like the tale repeated to the child’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 28

13.28

इत्यादिभिरुपाख्यानैर्मायाशक्तेस्तु विस्तरम्। वसिष्ठः कथयामास सैव शक्तिर्निरूप्यते॥

By such entertaining tales Vasiṣṭha described the power of Māyā. This power is now being described more fully.

Chapter 13 · Verse 29

13.29

कार्यादाश्रयतः सैषा भवेच्छक्तिर्विलक्षणा। स्फोटाङ्गारौ दृश्यमानौ शक्तिस्तत्रानुमीयते॥

This power is different both from its effect and also from its substratum. The blister (which is the effect) and the charcoal (the substratum) are cognised objects; but the power to burn is inferred from the effect (viz., the blister).

Chapter 13 · Verse 30

13.30

पृथुबुध्नोदराकारो घटः कार्योऽत्र मृत्तिका। शब्दादिभिः पञ्चगुणैर्युक्ता शक्तिस्त्वतद्विधा॥

The pot with its properties of thickness, roundness and so forth, is the product of power acting on the clay with its five properties of sound, touch, form, taste and smell, but the power is different here (from both the pot and the clay).

Chapter 13 · Verse 31

13.31

न पृथ्वादिर्न शब्दादिः शक्तावस्तु यथा तथा। अत एव ह्यचिन्त्यैषा न निर्वचनमर्हति॥

In the power (that creates the pot) there is neither form nor quality; as it is it remains (even when it has produced the effect, it undergoes no change). It is therefore said to be beyond thought and description.

Chapter 13 · Verse 32

13.32

कार्योत्पत्तेः पुरा शक्तिर्निगूढा मृद्यवस्थिता। कुलालादिसहायेन विकाराकारतां व्रजेत्॥

Before the creation of the pot, the power (of giving rise to a pot) is implicit in the clay. With the help of the potter and other means the clay is transformed into a pot.

Chapter 13 · Verse 33

13.33

पृथ्व्यादि विकारान्तं स्पर्शादिगुणमृत्तिकाम्। एकीकृत्य घटं प्राहुर्विचारविकला जनाः॥

People of immature minds confound the properties of the effect with those of the cause, the clay and speak of it as the pot.

Chapter 13 · Verse 34

13.34

कुलालव्यापृतेः पूर्वो यावानंश स नो घटः। पश्चात्तु पृथुबुध्नादिमत्त्वे युक्ता हि कुम्भता॥

The clay, before the potter worked on it, cannot be called a pot. But it is proper to call it a pot when it acquires the properties such as thickness, hollowness and so forth.

Chapter 13 · Verse 35

13.35

स घटो न मृदो भिन्नो वियोगे सत्यनीक्षणात्। नाप्यभिन्नः पुरा पिण्डदशायामनवेक्षणात्॥

The pot is not different from the clay, as it has no existence apart from the clay; it is neither identical with the clay, as in the unmoulded clay it is not perceived.

Chapter 13 · Verse 36

13.36

अतोऽनिर्वचनीयोऽयं शक्तिवत्तेन शक्तिजः। अव्यक्तव्ये शक्तिरुक्ता व्यक्तत्ये घटनामभृत्॥

Therefore the pot (a product of power) can only be called indescribable, like the power which produces it. Hence the product of power when imperceptible is simply called power and when perceptible it is called a pot.

Chapter 13 · Verse 37

13.37

ऐन्द्रजालिकनिष्ठापि माया न व्यज्यते पुरा। पश्चाद्गन्धर्वसेनादिरूपेण व्यक्तिमाप्नुयात्॥

A magician’s power is not apparent earlier; it is only when he brings it into operation that it appears as an army of Gandharvas and the like.

Chapter 13 · Verse 38

13.38

एवं मायामयत्वेन विकारस्यानृतात्मताम्। विकाराधारमृद्वस्तुसत्यत्वं चाब्रवीच्छ्रुतिः॥

Thus being illusive, in the scriptures, the products of power are called unreal whereas reality is predicated only of the entity in which the power inheres, e.g., of the clay in which the pot inheres.

Chapter 13 · Verse 39

13.39

वाङ्निष्पाद्यं नाममात्रं विकारो नास्य सत्यता। स्पर्शादि गुणयुक्ता तु सत्या केवलमृत्तिका॥

A pot taken as a product of power is only a name composed of words; it is not a real entity. Only the clay that possesses sound, touch, form, taste and smell, is a real entity.

Chapter 13 · Verse 40

13.40

व्यक्ताव्यक्ते तदाधार इति त्रिष्वाद्ययोर्द्वयोः। पर्यायः कालभेदेन तृतीयस्त्वनुगच्छति॥

Of the three entities, the manifest (i.e., product of power), the unmanifest (i.e., the power itself), and the substratum in which they both inhere, the first two exist by turns (thus cancelling one another); but the third persists in both (and at all times).

Chapter 13 · Verse 41

13.41

निस्तत्त्वं भासमानं च व्यक्तमुत्पत्तिनाशभाक्। तदुत्पत्तौ तस्य नाम वाचा निष्पाद्यते नृभिः॥

A product of power though visible has no real substance, as it is subject to creation and destruction. When it appears, it is given a name by men.

Chapter 13 · Verse 42

13.42

व्यक्ते नष्टेऽपि नामैतन्नृवक्त्रेष्वनुवर्तते। तेन नाम्ना निरूप्यत्वाद्व्यक्तं तद्रूपमुच्यते॥

When the product perishes, its name continues to be used by men. Since it is indicated only by name, it is said to be of nominal existence.

Chapter 13 · Verse 43

13.43

निस्तत्त्वत्वाद्विनाशित्वाद्वाचारम्भणनामतः। व्यक्तस्य न तु तद्रूपं सत्यं किञ्चिन्मृदादिवत्॥

This form of the product (of power, like the pot) is not real like clay, because it is unsubstantial, destructible and a mere name based upon words.

Chapter 13 · Verse 44

13.44

व्यक्तकाले ततः पूर्वमूर्ध्वमप्येकरूपभाक्। सतत्त्वमविनाशं च सत्यं मृद्वस्तु कथ्यते॥

The substance clay is said to be the real entity because by nature it is unchanged, substantial and indestructible at all times, before the production of the pot, after its destruction and even while it is manifest.

Chapter 13 · Verse 45

13.45

व्यक्तं घटो विकारश्चेत्येतैर्नामभिरीरितः। अर्थश्चेदनृतः कस्मान्न मृद्बोधे निवर्तते॥

(Doubt): If the thing indicated by the three terms i.e., the manifest, the pot and the modified form is unreal, why is it not destroyed when the knowledge of its substratum (clay) dawns?

Chapter 13 · Verse 46

13.46

निवृत्त एव यस्मात्ते तत्सत्यत्वमतिर्गता। ईदृङ्निवृत्तिरेवात्र बोधजा न त्वभासनम्॥

(Reply): With the knowledge of the substratum the pot is destroyed, for your idea of the reality of the pot is removed. This is what is meant by the destruction of the pot through knowledge; it does not mean that the pot would cease to appear.

Chapter 13 · Verse 47

13.47

पुमानधोमुखः नीरे भातोऽप्यस्ति न वस्तुतः। तटस्थमर्त्यवत्तस्मिन्नैवास्था कस्यचित्क्वचित्॥

Though a man appears head downwards when reflected in water, he is not so. No one would ever mistake it for the real person standing on the bank.

Chapter 13 · Verse 48

13.48

ईदृग्बोधे पुमर्थत्वं मतमद्वैतवादिनाम्। मृद्रूपस्यापरित्यागाद्विवर्तत्वं घटे स्थितम्॥

According to the doctrine of the non-dualists, such knowledge (i.e., the knowledge of the unreality of the superimposed thing, the world), gives liberation, the supreme goal of life. As the substratum clay is not rejected, the appearance of a pot in it is accepted.

Chapter 13 · Verse 49

13.49

परिणामे पूर्वरूपं त्यजेत्तत्क्षीररूपवत्। मृत्सुवर्णे निवर्तेते घटकुण्डलयोर्न हि॥

In an actual modification of the substratum, when milk is turned into curd (for example), the former form, milk, disappears. But in the modification of clay into a pot or gold into an ear-ring, the substratum does not change.

Chapter 13 · Verse 50

13.50

घटे नष्टे न मृद्भावः कपालानामवेक्षणात्। मैवं चूर्णेऽस्ति मृद्रूपं स्वर्णरूपं त्वतिस्फुटम्॥

(Doubt): When a pot is broken into pieces, they do not resemble the original clay, for broken pieces only are seen. (Reply): It is not so, for when reduced to powder they do. The persistence of gold in the ear-ring is very clear.

Chapter 13 · Verse 51

13.51

क्षीरादौ परिणामोऽस्तु पुनस्तद्भाववर्जनात्। एतावता मृदादीनां दृष्टान्तत्वं न हीयते॥

When milk is turned into curd, actual change of substance takes place. Milk ceases to exist as such and cannot be recovered from the curd. By this, the case of a clay-pot or a gold-ring (as examples of Vivarta) does not suffer.

Chapter 13 · Verse 52

13.52

आरम्भवादिनः कार्ये मृदो द्वैगुण्यमापतेत्। रूपस्पर्शादयः प्रोक्ताः कार्य कारणयोः पृथक्॥

According to the Ārambha-vādins, clay should have two sets of properties, viz., those of the cause and those of the effect, for they hold, the properties of the effects are different from those of the cause, which is, however, not the case.

Chapter 13 · Verse 53

13.53

मृत्सुवर्णमयश्चेति दृष्टान्तत्रयमारुणिः। प्राहातो वासयेत्कार्यानृतत्वं सर्ववस्तुषु॥

The sage Āruṇi (Uddālaka) mentions the three examples of clay, gold and iron (only to show that all effects are only phenomenal). Therefore one should fix in mind the unreality of all effects.

Chapter 13 · Verse 54

13.54

कारणज्ञानतः कार्यविज्ञानं चापि सोऽवदत्। सत्यज्ञानेऽनृतज्ञां कथमत्रोपपद्यते॥

Āruṇi holds that a knowledge of the cause implies a knowledge of all its effects. But how would a knowledge of the unreal effects arise from a knowledge of their real cause?

Chapter 13 · Verse 55

13.55

समृत्कस्य विकारस्य कार्यता लोकदृष्टितः। वास्तवोऽत्र मृदंशोऽस्य बोधः कारणबोधतः॥

According to the common view, an effect, such as a pot, is a modification of its material cause, clay; the clay portion of the pot is the real substance. Therefore when the cause of the pot is known, the real portion of substance of the pot is also known.

Chapter 13 · Verse 56

13.56

अनृतांशो न बोद्धव्यस्तद्बोधानुपयोगतः। तत्त्वज्ञानं पुमर्थं स्यान्नानृत अंशावबोधनम्॥

The unreal portion of the effect need not be known, because its knowledge serves no useful purpose. A knowledge of the real substance is necessary for men, whereas a knowledge of the unreal portion is useless.

Chapter 13 · Verse 57

13.57

तर्हि कारणविज्ञानात्कर्यज्ञामितीरिते। मृद्बोधान्मृत्तिका बुद्धेत्युक्तं स्यात्कोऽत्र विस्मयः॥

(Doubt): The statement that through the knowledge of the cause you arrive at a knowledge of the effect amounts to saying that by a knowledge of clay you acquire a knowledge of clay. What is there wonderful about it?

Chapter 13 · Verse 58

13.58

सत्यं कार्येषु वस्त्वंशः कारणात्मेति जानतः। विस्मयो मास्त्विहाज्ञस्य विस्मयः केन वार्यते॥

(Reply): The real substance in the effect (pot) is identical with its cause. This may not be surprising to the wise but who can prevent the ignorant being surprised at this?

Chapter 13 · Verse 59

13.59

आरम्भी परिणामी च लौकिकश्चैककारणे। ज्ञाते सर्वमतं श्रुत्वा प्राप्नुवन्त्येव विस्मयम्॥

The followers of Ārambha-vāda and Pariṇāma-vāda and ordinary men may find it puzzling to hear that a knowledge of the cause should give a knowledge of all its effects.

Chapter 13 · Verse 60

13.60

अद्वैतेऽभिमुखीकर्तुमेवात्रैकस्य बोधतः। सर्वबोधः श्रुतौ नैव नानात्वस्य विवक्षया॥

To direct the attention of the pupil to the non-dual truth, the Chāndogya Upaniṣad teaches that by a knowledge of the one cause all its effects are known. It does not speak of the multiplicity of effects.

Chapter 13 · Verse 61

13.61

एकमृत्पिण्डविज्ञानात्सर्वमृण्मयधीर्यथा। तथैकब्रह्मबोधेन जगद्बुद्धिर्विभाव्यताम्॥

Just by knowing a lump of clay one knows all objects made of clay, so by knowing the one Brahman one knows (the real element of) the whole phenomenal world.

Chapter 13 · Verse 62

13.62

सच्चित्सुखात्मकं ब्रह्म नामरूपात्मकं जगत्। तापनीये श्रुतं ब्रह्म सच्चिदानन्दलक्षणम्॥

The nature of Brahman is existence, consciousness and bliss, whereas the nature of the world is name and form. In the Nṛsiṃha-Uttara-Tāpanīya Upaniṣad existence, consciousness and bliss are said to be the ‘indications’ of Brahman.

Chapter 13 · Verse 63

13.63

सद्रूपमारुणिः प्राह प्रज्ञानं ब्रह्म बह्वृचाः। सनत्कुमार आनन्दमेवमन्यत्र गम्यताम्॥

Āruṇi described Brahman as of the nature of existence, the Bahv-ṛcas of the Ṛg-Veda as consciousness and Sanat-kumāra as bliss. The same is declared in other Upaniṣads.

Chapter 13 · Verse 64

13.64

विचिन्त्य सर्वरूपाणि कृत्वा नामानि तिष्ठति। अहं व्याकरवाणीमे नामरूपे इति श्रुतिः॥

After creating names and forms Brahman remains established in His nature, i.e., remains as immutable as ever, says the Puruṣa Sūkta. Another Śruti says that Brahman as the Self reveals names and forms.

Chapter 13 · Verse 65

13.65

अव्याकृतं पुरा सृष्टेरूर्ध्वं व्याक्रीयते द्विधा। अचिन्त्यशक्तिर्मायैषा ब्रह्मण्यव्याकृताभिधा॥

Another Śruti says that before creation the universe was unmanifest and that afterwards it became manifest as name and form. Here Māyā, the inexplicable power of Brahman, is referred to as ‘unmanifest’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 66

13.66

अविक्रियब्रह्मनिष्ठा विकारं यात्यनेकधा। मायां तु प्रकृतिं विद्यान्मायिनं तु महेश्वरम्॥

This Māyā, which rests unmanifest in the immutable Brahman, subsequently undergoes numerous modifications. ‘Know Māyā as Prakṛti (the material cause of the universe), and the supreme Lord as the Ruler (substratum) of Māyā’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 67

13.67

आद्यो विकार आकाशः सोऽस्ति भात्यपि च प्रियः। अवकाशस्तस्य रूपं तन्मिथ्या न तु तत्त्रयम्॥

The first modification of Māyā is Ākāśa; it exists, is manifest and is dear to all. The special form of Ākāśa is space which is unreal, but its other three properties (derived from its cause, Brahman), are not unreal.

Chapter 13 · Verse 68

13.68

न व्यक्तेः पूर्वमस्त्येव न पश्चाच्च विनाशतः। आदावन्ते च यन्नास्ति वर्तमानेऽपि तत्तथा॥

The spatial property does not exist before manifestation and ceases also to exist after destruction. That which is non-existent before creation and after dissolution is so even in the present (i.e., during creation).

Chapter 13 · Verse 69

13.69

अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत। अव्यक्तनिधनानीवेत्याह कृष्णोऽर्जुनं प्रति॥

Śrī Kṛṣṇa said to Arjuna: ‘O descendant of Bhārata, beings are unmanifest in the beginning, manifest in the present and unmanifest again at the end’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 70

13.70

मृद्वत्ते सच्चिदानन्दा अनुगच्छन्ति सर्वद। निराकाशे सदादीनामनुभूतिर्निजात्मनि॥

Just as clay exists (in its modifications such as the pot) in all the three divisions of time, so existence, consciousness and bliss ever pervade the Ākāśa, when the idea of space is negated from Ākāśa, what remains is one’s own Self-existence, consciousness and bliss (infinity).

Chapter 13 · Verse 71

13.71

अवकाशे विस्मृतेऽथ तत्र किं भाति ते वद। शून्यमेवेति चेदस्तु नाम तादृग्विभाति हि॥

When the idea of space is negated from Ākāśa, what remains of it? If you say, ‘Nothing remains’, we accept it and say that that which is represented by the word ‘nothing’ is revealed.

Chapter 13 · Verse 72

13.72

तादृक्त्वादेव तत्सत्त्वमौदासीन्येन तत्सुखम्। आनुकूल्यप्रातिकूल्यहीनं यत्तन्निजं सुखम्॥

Because it is such that we must attribute existence to the remaining entity. Being productive of no misery, it is bliss, for the absence of both the favourable and the unfavourable is the bliss of the Self.

Chapter 13 · Verse 73

13.73

आनुकूल्ये हर्षधीः स्यात्प्रातिकूल्ये तु दुःखधीः। द्वयाभावे निजानन्दो निजं दुःखं तु न क्वचित्॥

One gets pleasure from a favourable object and grief from an unfavourable one; but in the natural state, free from both, there is the natural bliss of the Self. There is never any experience of misery in that state.

Chapter 13 · Verse 74

13.74

निजानन्दे स्थिते हर्षशोकयोर्व्यत्ययः क्षणात्। मनसः क्षणिकत्वेन तयोर्मानसतेष्यताम्॥

The natural bliss of the Self is uniform and steady, but the mind due to its fickle nature, passes in a moment from joy to sorrow. So both are to be looked upon as the creations of the mind.

Chapter 13 · Verse 75

13.75

आकाशेऽप्येवमानन्दः सत्ताभाने तु संमते। वाय्वादिदेहपर्यन्तवस्तुष्वेवं विभाव्यताम्॥

Thus in Ākāśa also we accept bliss, i.e., it is fundamentally existence, consciousness and bliss and similarly we can establish that the fundamental nature of all objects from air to the physical body is essentially the same.

Chapter 13 · Verses 76–77

13.76–77

गतिस्पर्शौ वायुरूपं वह्नेर्दाहप्रकाशने। जलस्य द्रवता भूमेः काठिन्यं चेति निर्णयः॥ असाधारण आकाशे ओषध्यन्नवपुःष्वपि। एवं विभाव्य मनसा तत्तद्रूपं यथोचितम्॥

The special properties of air have been determined as motion and touch; of fire, heat and light; of water, liquidity; and of earth, solidity. Similarly the special properties of plants, foods, bodies and other objects can be thought of by the mind.

Chapter 13 · Verse 78

13.78

अनेकधा विभिन्नेषु नामरूपेषु चैकधा। तिष्ठन्ति सच्चिदानन्दाविसंवादः न कस्यचित्॥

In the manifold objects, different in names and forms, the common element is existence, consciousness and bliss. Nobody can dispute this.

Chapter 13 · Verse 79

13.79

निस्तत्त्वे नामरूपे द्वे जन्मनाशयुते च ते। बुद्ध्या ब्रह्मणि वीक्षस्व समुद्रे बुद्बुदादिवत्॥

Both name and form are without any real existence because they are subject to creation and destruction. So know them as superimposed by the intellect on Brahman, just as waves and foam are on the ocean.

Chapter 13 · Verse 80

13.80

सच्चिदानन्दरूपेऽस्मिन् पूर्णे ब्रह्मणि वीक्षिते। स्वयमेवावजानाति नामरूपे शनैः शनैः॥

With the direct knowledge of Brahman, the eternal existence, consciousness and bliss, names and forms slowly come to be disregarded.

Chapter 13 · Verse 81

13.81

यावद्यावदवज्ञा स्यात्तावत्तावत्तदीक्षणम्। यावद्यावद्वीक्ष्यते तत्तावत्तावदुभे त्यजेत्॥

The more is duality negated, the clearer does the realisation of Brahman become and as realisation becomes perfect, names and forms come to be disregarded of themselves.

Chapter 13 · Verse 82

13.82

तदभ्यासेन विद्यायां सुस्थितायामयं पुमान्। जीवन्नेव भवेन्मुक्तो वपुरस्तु यथा तथा॥

When through the continuous practice of meditation a man is established in the knowledge of Brahman, he becomes liberated even while living. Then the fate of his body does not matter.

Chapter 13 · Verse 83

13.83

तच्चिन्तनं तत्कथनमन्योन्यं तत्प्रबोधनम्। एतदेकपरत्वं च तदभ्यासं विदुर्बुधाः॥

Thinking of Him, speaking of Him and making one another understand Him – this is what the wise call ‘practice of Brahman-realisation’.

Chapter 13 · Verse 84

13.84

वासनानेककालिना दीर्घकालं निरन्तरम्। सादरं चाभ्यस्यमाने सर्वथैव निवर्तते॥

The longstanding impressions of the world on the mind are loosened if this training of knowledge is constantly practised with earnestness for a long time.

Chapter 13 · Verse 85

13.85

मृच्छक्तिवद्ब्रह्मशक्तिरनेकाननृतान्सृजेत्। यद्वा जीवगता निद्रा स्वप्नश्चात्र निदर्शनम्॥

As the power inherent in the clay brings the pot into existence, so the power of Māyā inherent in Brahman creates many unreal things. This is illustrated by sleep and dream conditions of living beings.

Chapter 13 · Verse 86

13.86

निद्राशक्तिर्यथा जीवे दुर्घटस्वप्नकारिणी। ब्रह्मण्येषा तथा माया सृष्टिस्थित्यन्तकारिणी॥

Just as in the sleeping state a power inherent in the Jīva gives rise to impossible dreams, so the power of Māyā inherent in Brahman, projects, maintains and destroys the universe.

Chapter 13 · Verse 87

13.87

स्वप्ने वियद्गतिं पश्येत्स्वमूर्धच्छेदनं यथा। मुहूर्ते वत्सरौघं च मृतं पुत्रादिकं पुनः॥

In dream a man may see himself flying in the sky or being beheaded. In a moment he may live through the experience of many years. Or he may dream of seeing a dead son and so forth.

Chapter 13 · Verse 88

13.88

इदं युक्तमिदं नेति व्यवस्था तत्र दुर्लभा। यथा यथेक्ष्यते यद्यत्तत्तद्युक्तं तथा तथा॥

‘This is proper (possible) and this is not’ such discrimination is not possible then. Whatever one perceives in dreams seems to be in the right place.

Chapter 13 · Verse 89

13.89

ईदृशो महिमा दृष्टो निद्राशक्तेर्यदा तदा। मायाशक्तेरचिन्त्योऽयं महिमेति किमद्भुतम्॥

When such is the glory of the power of sleep and dream, what is there to wonder at the unimaginable glory of the power of Māyā?

Chapter 13 · Verse 90

13.90

शयाने पुरुषे निद्रा स्वप्नं बहुविधं सृजेत्। ब्रह्मण्येवं निर्विकारे विकारान्कल्पयत्यसौ॥

In a sleeping man various dreams are created; similarly the power of Māyā creates diverse appearances in the immutable Brahman.

Chapter 13 · Verse 91

13.91

खानिलाग्निजलोर्व्यण्डलोकप्राणिशिलादिकाः। विकाराः प्राणिधीष्वन्तश्चिच्छाया प्रतिबिम्बति॥

Ākāśa, air, fire, water, earth, the universe, the different Lokas (worlds) and animate and inanimate objects are appearances produced by Māyā. Pure consciousness appears as a reflection in the intellects of living beings.

Chapter 13 · Verse 92

13.92

चेतनाचेतनेष्वेषु सच्चिदानन्दलक्षणम्। समानं ब्रह्म भिद्येते नामरूपे पृथक्पृथक्॥

Brahman characterised as existence, consciousness and bliss is the common basis of both the animate and inanimate objects; they differ only in their names and forms.

Chapter 13 · Verse 93

13.93

ब्रह्मण्येते नामरूपे पटे चित्रमिव स्थिते। उपेक्ष्य नामरूपे द्वे सच्चिदानन्दधीर्भवेत्॥

Just as many objects are seen in a picture, so the various names and forms exist in Brahman. By negating both names and forms, one can understand that what remains is existence, consciousness and bliss.

Chapter 13 · Verse 94

13.94

जलस्थेऽधोमुखे स्वस्य देहे दृष्टेऽप्युपेक्ष्य तम्। तीरस्थ एव देहे स्वे तात्पर्यं स्याद्यथा तथा॥

Even though a man standing on the bank of a river sees his body reflected upside down in the water, he nevertheless identifies himself with his own body in the shore; similarly an aspirant after realisation of Brahman should know himself as Brahman.

Chapter 13 · Verse 95

13.95

सहस्रशो मनोराज्ये वर्तमाने सदैव तत्। सर्वैरूपेक्ष्यते तद्वदुपेक्षा नामरूपयोः॥

Just as in day-dreaming, people see thousands of mental pictures, but in the practical world they disregard them all, so should names and forms be disregarded.

Chapter 13 · Verse 96

13.96

क्षणे क्षणे मनोराज्यं भवत्येवान्यथान्यथा। गतं गतं पुनर्नास्ति व्यवहारो बहिस्तथा॥

Different mental creations are formed every moment, while those which pass are lost for ever. The objects of the practical world should be looked upon similarly.

Chapter 13 · Verse 97

13.97

न बाल्यं यौवने लभ्यं यौवनं स्थविरे तथा। मृतः पिता पुनर्नास्ति नायात्येव गतं दिनम्॥

Childhood is lost in youth and youth is lost in old age. The father once dead does not return. The day which is past never comes back.

Chapter 13 · Verse 98

13.98

मनोराज्याद्विशेषः कः क्षणध्वंसिनि लौकिके। अतोऽस्मिन्भासमानेऽपि तत्सत्यत्वधियं त्यजेत्॥

How do the objects of the practical world, which are destroyed every moment, differ from the forms created by the mind in imagination? Though they appear, the idea of their reality should be given up.

Chapter 13 · Verse 99

13.99

उपेक्षिते लौकिके धीर्निर्विघ्ना ब्रह्मचिन्तने। नटवत्कृत्रिमास्थायां निर्वहत्येव लौकिकम्॥

When the objects of the world are disregarded, the mind freed from obstacles rests in the contemplation of Brahman. Then like an actor, a wise man is engaged in worldly concerns with assumed faith (and so is not affected by them).

Chapter 13 · Verse 100

13.100

प्रवहत्यपि नीरेऽधः स्थिरा प्रौढ शिला यथा। नामरूपान्यथात्वेऽपि कूटस्थं ब्रह्म नान्यथा॥

As the big rock lying in the bed of a river remains unmoved, though the water flows over it, so also while names and forms constantly change, the unchanging Brahman does not become otherwise.

Chapter 13 · Verse 101

13.101

निष्छिद्रे दर्पणे भाति वस्तुगर्भं बृहद्वियत्। सच्चित्घने तथा नानाजगद्गर्भमिदं वियत्॥

As the sky with all its contents is reflected in a flawless mirror, so the Ākāśa with all the universe within it is reflected on the one partless Brahman, who is nothing but absolute consciousness and existence.

Chapter 13 · Verse 102

13.102

अदृष्ट्वा दर्पणं नैव तदन्तस्थे क्षणं यथा। अमत्वा सच्चिदानन्दं नामरूपमतिः कुतः॥

Without seeing the mirror it is impossible to see the objects reflected in it. Similarly wherefrom can there be any knowledge of names and forms without a knowledge of their substratum, which is existence, consciousness and bliss?

Chapter 13 · Verse 103

13.103

प्रथमं सच्चिदानन्दे भासमानेऽथ तावता। बुद्धिं नियम्य नैवोर्ध्वं धारयेन्नामरूपयोः॥

Having learnt of Brahman as existence, consciousness and bliss, one should fix the mind firmly on Him and should restrain it from dwelling on names and forms.

Chapter 13 · Verse 104

13.104

एवं च निर्जगद्ब्रह्म सच्चिदानन्दलक्षणम्। अद्वैतानन्द एतस्मिन्विश्राम्यन्तु जनाश्चिरम्॥

Thus Brahman is realised as existence, consciousness and bliss and devoid of the phenomenal universe. May all people find rest in this secondless bliss of Brahman.

Chapter 13 · Verse 105

13.105

ब्रह्मानन्दाभिधे ग्रन्थे तृतीयेऽध्याय ईरितः। अद्वैतानन्द एव स्याज्जगन्मिथ्यात्वचिन्तया॥

In this third chapter of the section called ‘the Bliss of Brahman’, is described the bliss of Non-duality which is to be obtained by meditating on the unreality of the world.

Chapter 14

Chapter 14 · Verse 1

14.1

योगेनात्मविवेकेन द्वैतमिथ्यात्वचिन्तया। ब्रह्मानन्दं पश्यतोऽथ विद्यानन्दो निरूप्यते॥

Now is being described the bliss of knowledge experienced by him who has realised the bliss of Brahman through Yoga, discrimination of the Self and thinking of the unreality of duality.

Chapter 14 · Verse 2

14.2

विषयानन्दवद्विद्यानन्दोधीवृत्तिरूप्कः। दुःखाभावादिरूपेण प्रोक्त एष चतुर्विधः॥

Like the bliss arising from the contact of the mind with external objects, the bliss arising from the knowledge of Brahman is a modification of the intellect. It is said to have four aspects, in the forms of absence of sorrow etc.

Chapter 14 · Verse 3

14.3

दुःखाभावश्च कामाप्तिः कृतकृत्योऽहमित्यसौ। प्राप्तप्राप्योऽहमित्येवं चातुर्विध्यमुदाहृतम्॥

The four aspects of the bliss of knowledge are: absence of sorrow, the fulfilment of all desires, the feeling ‘I have done all that was to be done’, and also the feeling ‘I have achieved all that was to be achieved’.

Chapter 14 · Verse 4

14.4

ऐहिकं च आमुष्मिकं चेत्येवं दुःखं द्विधेरितम्। निवृत्तिमैहिकस्याह बृहदारण्यकं वचः॥

Sorrow is twofold, that of this world and that of the next. The cessation of the sorrow of this world has been described in the words of the Bṛhad-āraṇyaka Upaniṣad.

Chapter 14 · Verse 5

14.5

आत्मानं चेद्विजानीयादयमस्मीति पूरुषः। किमिच्छन्कस्य कामाय शरीरमनुसंज्वरेत्॥

‘When a man (Puruṣa) has realised the identity of his own Self with That (Paramātman), desiring what and to please whom should he allow his body and mind to be afflicted?’

Chapter 14 · Verse 6

14.6

जीवात्मा परमात्मा चेत्यात्मा द्विविध ईरितः। चित्तादात्म्यात्त्रिभिर्देहैर्जीवः सन्भोक्तृतां व्रजेत्॥

The Self is spoken of as of two types: the individual Self and the supreme Self. The consciousness, through identification with the three bodies, thinks itself as the Jīva and becomes an enjoyer.

Chapter 14 · Verse 7

14.7

परमात्मा सच्चिदानन्दस्तादात्म्यं नामरूपयोः। गत्वा भोग्यत्वमापन्नस्तद्विवेके तु नोभयम्॥

The supreme Self, who is by nature existence, consciousness and bliss, identifying itself with names and forms becomes the objects of enjoyment. When by discrimination it is disidentified from the three bodies and names and forms, there is neither the enjoyer nor anything to be enjoyed.

Chapter 14 · Verse 8

14.8

भोग्यमिच्छन्भोक्तुरर्थे शरीरमनुसंज्वरेत्। ज्वरास्त्रिषु शरीरेषु स्थिता न त्वात्मनो ज्वराः॥

Desiring the objects of enjoyment for the sake of the enjoyer, the Jīva suffers, being identified with the body. The sufferings are in the three bodies, but there are no sufferings for the Self.

Chapter 14 · Verse 9

14.9

व्याधयो धातुवैषम्ये स्थूलदेहे स्थिता ज्वराः। कामक्रोधादयः सूक्ष्मे द्वयोर्बीजं तु कारणे॥

The diseases due to the disequilibrium of the bodily humours are the suffering of the gross body; desire, anger etc., are the suffering of the subtle body; and the source of the sufferings of both the gross and subtle bodies is the suffering of the causal body.

Chapter 14 · Verse 10

14.10

अद्वैतानन्दमार्गेण परात्मनि विवेचिते। अपश्यन्वास्तवं भोग्यं किं नामेच्छेत्परात्मवित्॥

The knower of the supreme Self, while discriminating about it as mentioned in the Chapter on the ‘Bliss of Non-duality’, sees no reality in any object of enjoyment. What then should he desire?

Chapter 14 · Verse 11

14.11

आत्मानन्दोक्तरीत्यास्मिन्जीवात्मन्यवधारिते। भोक्ता नैवास्ति कोऽप्यत्र शरीरानुज्वरः कुतः॥

When the individual Self is determined (to be identical with the immutable) through the methods mentioned in Chapter 12 on the ‘Bliss of the Self’, there remains no enjoyer in this body. So how can there be sufferings which are the result of identification with the body?

Chapter 14 · Verse 12

14.12

पुण्यपापद्वये चिन्ता दुःखमामुष्मिकं भवेत्। प्रथमाध्याय एवोक्तं चिन्ता नैनं तपेदिति॥

Anxiety regarding virtue and vice are the sufferings of the future life. It has already been told in Chapter 11 that such anxiety cannot affect the illumined man.

Chapter 14 · Verse 13

14.13

यथा पुष्करपर्णेऽस्मिन्नपामश्लेषणं तथा। वेदनादूर्ध्वमागामिकर्मणोऽश्लेषणं बुधे॥

As water does not stick to the leaves of a lotus so after realisation future actions cannot stick to the knower.

Chapter 14 · Verse 14

14.14

इषीकातृणतूलस्य वह्निदाहः क्षणाद्यथा। तथा सञ्चितकर्मास्य दग्धं भवति वेदनात्॥

Just as the cotton-like flowers of the Iṣīkā reed are burnt by fire in a moment, so the accumulated past actions of the knower are burnt up because of realisation.

Chapter 14 · Verse 15

14.15

यथैधांसि समिद्धोऽग्निर्भस्मसात्कुरुतेऽर्जुन। ज्ञानाग्निः सर्वकर्माणि भस्मसात्कुरुते तथा॥

Śrī Kṛṣṇa says: ‘Just as a blazing fire reduces the fuel to ashes, so, O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge burns up all actions’.

Chapter 14 · Verse 16

14.16

यस्य नाहंकृतो भावो बुद्धिर्यस्य न लिप्यते। हत्वापि स इमां लोकान्न हन्ति न निबध्यते॥

‘He who has no notion of I-ness and whose mind is not tainted by desire for results of action is not really a killer even if he kills people; he is not bound by his actions’.

Chapter 14 · Verse 17

14.17

मातापित्रोर्वधः स्तेयं भ्रूणहत्यान्यदीदृशम्। न मुक्तिं नाशयेत्पापं मुखकान्तिर्न नश्यति॥

In the Kauśītaki Upaniṣad it is said that killing of parents, stealing, causing abortion and such other sins do not affect his illumination, nor is the colour (serenity) of his countenance marred.

Chapter 14 · Verse 18

14.18

दुःखाभाववदेवास्य सर्वकामाप्तिरीरिता। सर्वान्कामानसावाप्य ह्यमृतो भवदित्यतः॥

It has been said in the Aitareya Upaniṣad that like the cessation of all sorrows, the knower achieves all the desired objects also: ‘He becomes immortal, achieving all the desired objects’.

Chapter 14 · Verse 19

14.19

जक्षन्क्रीडन्रतिं प्राप्तः स्त्रीभिर्यानैस्तथेतरैः। शरीरं न स्मरेत्प्राणं कर्मणा जीवयेदमुम्॥

In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad it is said that the knower of Truth may be seen laughing, playing, rejoicing with women, vehicles and other things but he does not remember the body. The vital breath, impelled by his fructifying actions keeps him alive.

Chapter 14 · Verse 20

14.20

सर्वान्कामान्सहाप्नोति नान्यवज्जन्मकर्मभिः। वर्तन्ते श्रोत्रिये भोगा युगपत्क्रमवर्जिताः॥

‘The knower of Brahman attains fulfilment of all his desires’. For him unlike others, there are no enjoyments through rebirths and actions. His bliss is unqualified and immediate and devoid of sequence or degree.

Chapter 14 · Verses 21–22

14.21–22
